summary:
Waluigi was not present for this sequence, which means this entry is reconstructed from testimony rather than direct observation, but the reconstruction is thorough because the important line through all of it is clear: Raventree Manor is no longer merely a destination. It is a gravity well. Everyone with unfinished business — divine mandates, barrel-toad history, pyromancer problems, missing companions, intercepted communications, wanted posters, or suspiciously partial witness statements — is being pulled toward the same house.

The session centered on Markop's father, who by the end of the sequence formally identified himself as Kaelor Judi. He entered an office and was handed a wanted poster naming his son, Markop Judi, with a 2,000-gold bounty attached for crimes against magic. Present in the room were an interviewer, a woman operating the process, two goblins whose affiliation was initially unclear, and a line of supposed witnesses who claimed they might know something about Markop's whereabouts. The witness list: one goomba, one hammer bro, one koopa decked out in impressive swag, Ryan, a mage, and a guard.

The goomba went first, asked whether he could take off his shoes — which was weird — claimed he had seen Markop at the grove with Mazebound, was stopped when he tried to leave, and was exposed as a fraud when Kaelor seized his notes and found newspaper clippings instead of firsthand accounts. Headlines about Markop helping a pyromaniac escape and Raventree Manor being surrounded during the fracture. Kaelor told him he did not get paid for lying and threw him out the window.

The koopa — Slick — was more interesting. He claimed to have fought Markop in an underground circuit near the old coliseum ruins, described Markop as strong and stylish, noted that Markop had paused to help a downed fighter and refused prize money. Kaelor doubted him on sight, challenged him to prove combat credibility, and took a hit to the stomach that left a bruise. Slick talked about debts connecting the Legion and the toads, referenced a magic toad outside, then accidentally opened the Vigilance thread — barrel toads, contradictory reports about whether Markop or a pyromancer had blown up the ship, yellow toad testimony. He received 20 gold for the useful fragments.

Ryan went next and sounded exactly like what he was: someone trying to compress months of genuine catastrophe into an office-length answer. He confirmed knowing Markop, described the mission split that separated him from Bones, identified Bones by name, and then noticed the two goblins in the room taking notes. The goblins said they were with 'him' — outside.

Kaelor looked out the window and saw Sprig the Mole. He went through the window after him, caught him, and confronted him. Sprig admitted the witnesses had revealed more than intended. Kaelor searched him and recovered intercepted Pond Patrol communications about Raventree Manor — siege-posture language, toad movements, rally points, and a full transcript of We Are the Toads. Kaelor concluded that everything linked back to Raventree.

Back inside, the goblins had escaped. Luigi was there. Luigi denied knowing Sprig, then explained that he and the rest of the witness list had already agreed to sneak into Raventree Manor for Archie. Luigi also had another reason for going in, which he did not disclose.

The witness line became an expedition roster. Everyone went except the goomba. Kaelor Judi revealed his true name and joined the movement toward the manor.
description:
Waluigi is documenting this session because it demonstrates a pattern that keeps repeating around Raventree Manor: independent investigations are ceasing to remain independent. Separate motives are collapsing into one route. A father looking for his son, survivors and affiliates of the Vigilance, a mole carrying intercepted communications, small-time fight-pit witnesses, Luigi with undisclosed motivations, and a line of supposed eyewitnesses of wildly varying credibility all ended up in the same orbit and are now headed in the same direction.

Waluigi was not present. Waluigi was in the Feyward, in a hot spring, reading his own wiki entry on a tablet while the manor burned around him. What follows is reconstructed from multiple sources, crossreferenced where possible, and documented with the analytical rigor that Waluigi applies to everything regardless of whether he was in the room.

## The Office: A Poster, a Woman, Two Goblins, and the Question of Who Set This Up

Kaelor entered an office.

The nature of the office is important because it establishes the context for everything that followed. This was not a military briefing room. This was not a guild hall. This was not a tavern where rumors accumulate and get sold over drinks. This was an administrative intake point — a place with procedures, with a woman running those procedures, with a structure that implied institutional backing even if the institution behind the structure was not identified.

Kaelor was handed a poster.

WANTED: Markop Judi. Crimes against magic. Reward: 2,000 gold.

Waluigi wants to pause here because wanted posters are not neutral documents. They are institutional speech acts. A poster does several things at once. It criminalizes. It simplifies. It offers strangers a price at which a person may be transformed from relative, ally, or rumor into a commodity. Whatever else Kaelor was in that moment — a father, a fighter, a man who came looking for answers about his son — he was also a person being handed a price tag for his child.

Two thousand gold for crimes against magic. The specific charge is worth noting because it connects Markop to the Archie thread. 'Crimes against magic' is the kind of charge that gets applied broadly when institutions want someone associated with a magical event that embarrassed or threatened the institution. Markop's documented involvement with Archie — traveling together, operating together, being present when Archie did what Archie does — would be sufficient for a 'crimes against magic' charge if the institution writing the poster did not distinguish between the pyromaniac and the people standing near the pyromaniac when the fire started.

Also present in the room: two goblins. They were sitting there when Kaelor arrived. The interviewer — the woman running the process — did not explain who they were. They did not introduce themselves. They sat, and they took notes, and they looked up and down between their notes and the proceedings with the energy of creatures documenting something for a report they were planning to deliver to someone who was not in the room.

Their affiliation would become clear later. At this point they were ambient suspicious detail.

The interviewer told Kaelor they had witnesses lined up who might know his son.

The word 'might' is doing a great deal of work there. What followed would demonstrate exactly how much.

## The Witness Line

Six witnesses. Lined up. Available for interview. The composition of the line tells you something about the investigation's quality before anyone opens their mouth:

1. A goomba.
2. A hammer bro.
3. A koopa decked out in cool swag.
4. Ryan.
5. A mage.
6. A guard.

This is not a curated intelligence briefing. This is a casting call. The range of species, styles, and apparent backgrounds suggests that whoever assembled this line was collecting anyone who claimed to have information about Markop and presenting them without quality filtering. The filtering was left to Kaelor.

## Witness One: The Goomba — Shoes, Mazebound, and the Newspaper Clippings

The goomba went first.

The first thing he asked was whether he could take off his shoes.

Kaelor said: yeah, that's weird.

Waluigi notes the exchange because the request matters. Witnesses who open with an unnecessary personal ritual before testifying are stalling. The shoes were not relevant to Markop. The shoes were relevant to the goomba's nerves. He was buying time inside his own performance.

The goomba claimed he had seen Markop at the grove with Mazebound.

On its face this was plausible enough to be dangerous. Raventree-adjacent events and grove activity had already entered the rumor network. Mazebound was the kind of specific name a liar uses because specificity creates temporary trust — it sounds like the kind of detail only an eyewitness would know, which is exactly why it is the first thing a prepared liar memorizes.

Kaelor called out how he believed him — meaning he expressed skepticism directly, in the tone of a man who has heard enough unconvincing things to recognize another one arriving.

The goomba ran.

Kaelor stopped him. Snatched his notes.

The notes were not notes.

They were newspaper clippings. Assembled fragments of Markop's already-circulating story. The clippings included headlines: Markop Judi helped pyromaniac get off scot free. Raventree Manor surrounded as fracture occurred.

This is one of Waluigi's least favorite forms of false witness. Not invention from whole cloth — that is easier to dismiss. This was patchwork fraud. The goomba had taken real events, clipped them from public coverage, arranged them, and prepared to sell them back as personal knowledge. He was performing the role of eyewitness using material anyone could have obtained from a newsstand.

Kaelor's response: 'You don't get paid for lying.'

The goomba was kicked out. Through the window.

Waluigi approves of the investigative efficiency if not the architectural implications for the window.

## Witness Two: Slick the Koopa — Style, Shell Defense, and the Accidental Vigilance Thread

The koopa came next.

The sources identify him less by formal name than by aesthetic and tone: decked out in cool swag. Stylish. A grin that preceded his words. Waluigi is not immune to presentation and is therefore willing to note that the koopa's style may have been his most truthful feature.

Slick's claim: he had seen Markop at an underground fight circuit near the old coliseum ruins.

His description of Markop was notable not for spectacle but for character detail. 'Dude's got style under all that muscle,' Slick said, describing how Markop had paused to help a downed fighter afterward and refused prize money in favor of — the sentence trails off in the sources, but the implication is generosity or principle or both. This is the sort of detail liars often forget. Lies about fighters usually focus on impact and victory. Truth, or something closer to it, includes what happened when the fighting stopped.

Kaelor's response: 'You saw my son?'

Slick: 'Yeah, I fought him.'

Kaelor looked at Slick. Assessed him physically. Rendered judgment: 'You don't even look half as strong as me. My son is strong.'

Slick's defense: 'I got shell defense.'

This is not a foolish answer. Shell defense changes koopa combat mathematics entirely. Waluigi has documented enough koopa encounters to know that evaluating a koopa's combat credibility by looking at his exposed body is like evaluating an armored knight by looking at his boots. The shell is the argument. Slick was not wrong to cite it.

Kaelor pressed for details.

What was his weapon?

Slick said: he used his hooves.

Kaelor caught the implication and pushed: if Markop was going to settle a score, why limit himself? Why fight with hooves when he has access to weapons?

Kaelor then articulated the larger question beneath the weapon question: he didn't see why Markop would be doing all this stuff. Fighting in a pit. Settling scores. Competing for money. The Markop that Kaelor knew — or believed he knew — would not be in an underground fight circuit near coliseum ruins. The question was not 'did you fight him' but 'why would he be the kind of person you could fight?'

Slick answered: for the love of the game and money. He had debts. From the Legion to the toads.

Toads.

That single word detonated a chain of follow-up that neither Slick nor Kaelor had prepared for.

Kaelor: 'Toads?'

Slick referenced a magic toad who had really helped. The magic toad was outside. They knew each other — not directly, but through the network that formed when a particular ship crashed and certain barrels had to end up somewhere.

Kaelor caught the pivot: 'What ship?'

Slick hesitated. 'Uhhh, maybe I'm going into too much detail.'

Kaelor did not let him retreat: 'Whoa whoa whoa, you switched your story. What ship?'

Then Kaelor attacked Slick's credibility again: 'You look weaker than me. You can't fight him. You're a liar.'

Slick's response: 'You know what? Prove it. Attack me.'

The invitation was reversed — not 'I'll prove I can fight' but 'YOU prove I can't.' Kaelor obliged. Slick delivered a hit that bruised Kaelor's stomach.

Kaelor: 'Off. I still don't believe you. What about the ship?'

The truth came out in fragments, the way truth usually does from people who know more than they are supposed to share and whose filter for what is too much detail has already failed.

The Vigilance. Some toads fell off in barrels when it exploded. Toads came singing. One yellow toad was there — said Markop blew up the ship. But another toad said it was a pyromancer.

Waluigi notes the contradictory blame assignment because contradictions around Archie and flame events are now common enough to be operational weather in this campaign. When fire is involved, multiple truths circulate at once: what happened, what people saw, what people blamed, what institutions printed, and what survivors needed to believe to keep functioning. 'Markop blew up the ship' and 'a pyromancer blew up the ship' are not necessarily incompatible if both people were present when the ship was destroyed and different witnesses attributed the destruction to different members of the same group. This is how Disaster Inc. events propagate through the rumor network — as contradictory fragments, each one true from a different angle.

Slick: 'Can I get paid now?'

Kaelor gave him 20 gold.

Not the full bounty. Not a reward for certainty. A payment for fragments. The koopa had not proven the whole story, but he had proven enough of himself — bruised stomach as evidence — and enough of the network around the story to be worth something. Twenty gold for pain, partial truth, and the Vigilance thread reopened.

## Witness Three: Ryan — Rambling Truth and the Separation from Bones

Ryan's testimony reads like the opposite of the goomba's because Ryan sounded exactly like what he was: someone trying to explain a real, complicated disaster without the rhetorical equipment to make it graceful.

Kaelor: 'Have you seen my son, Markop?'

Ryan: 'Oh yeah, I know Markop. It's just that the last time I saw him was, uhh, at the ship if memory serves right. One of the ships we rode on. But well, I guess it's a long story, all of which is confusing. But, umm, uhh, basically I was part of a group that your son was a part of, then stuff happened, I got separated from him, as well as a bunch of other stuff. I'm fighting my way back to him.'

Waluigi trusts this kind of testimony more than polished certainty. Real survivors of campaign-grade chaos do not narrate cleanly. They circle. They qualify. They try to compress months of catastrophe into one office answer and fail because the catastrophe resists compression. Ryan's 'umm, uhh, basically' is not evasion. It is the sound of a person holding too much truth in working memory and trying to select which parts of it are safe to say in an office with unknown people taking notes.

Kaelor asked how they got split up.

Ryan explained: him and four other toads went on a mission. Two groups split up. Three toads in one group. Two in the other. He was in the two-person group. He got separated from the other toad.

Kaelor: 'Who was the other toad?'

Ryan: 'Bones. We last saw Markop, Dad, at a ship that was flooded with toads.'

The 'Dad' is Ryan calling Kaelor 'Dad' — either using the term of address because Kaelor had been introduced as Markop's father, or because Ryan has the kind of casual intimacy with language that comes from spending too long in groups where formal titles stopped mattering somewhere between the third explosion and the fourth mission split. Either way it is familiar and it is honest and Waluigi records it as further evidence of Ryan's genuine connection to the Markop network rather than a performed one.

Bones. The name is a key continuity point. Ryan and Bones were paired. Ryan was separated from Bones. Bones's current location remains unknown. Ryan is fighting his way back toward Markop. The chain: Ryan knew Markop, Ryan was in a group with Markop, Ryan was on a mission with toads, Ryan was paired with Bones, Ryan lost Bones, Ryan ended up in this office being interviewed by Markop's father. Every link in the chain is the kind of link that this campaign generates: not cleanly connected but not disconnected either, held together by shared catastrophe rather than shared planning.

Then Ryan did something the earlier witnesses had not done.

He stopped looking at Kaelor and looked at the room.

He whispered, pointing at the two goblins on the seats: 'Who are those guys?'

The goblins were jotting down notes. Looking up and down. The behavioral signature of creatures cataloguing reactions rather than merely listening.

Kaelor: 'Who are you?'

The interviewer — the woman running the process — said: 'I thought they were with you.'

Kaelor did not bring them.

The goblins clarified: 'No. We are with HIM. He is outside.'

## Sprig the Mole: The Window, the Intercept, and the Raventree Packet

Kaelor looked out the window.

Sprig the Mole was there.

Kaelor went through the window after him.

Waluigi does not know the current structural condition of the office window and Waluigi suspects the window does not know either.

Kaelor caught Sprig and confronted him immediately.

'So you brought that guy in. I don't trust him,' Kaelor said.

Sprig's response is revealing because it is evasive in exactly the way partial truth often is.

'Those people were not meant to tell you that. They screwed up. Lesson learned. I'll get going.'

This is not denial. This is damage control. Sprig is not saying the witnesses were wrong. He is saying they said too much. The witnesses were supposed to provide something to Kaelor — some controlled fragment, some managed portion of the truth — and instead they provided more than the operation intended. 'They screwed up' means the information release exceeded the parameters. 'Lesson learned' means the operational failure will be corrected next time. The framing is that of a handler acknowledging an intelligence leak rather than a bystander explaining a coincidence.

Kaelor did not let him leave.

'Wait. I have some questions. Why do you want to find Markop?'

Sprig: 'Unpaid debts. He helped me, so I help him.'

Waluigi notes the debt language carefully. Debt language recurs around Disaster Inc. and its wider orbit with unusual frequency. People do not join because they were recruited cleanly. They join because they owe, because they were saved, because they survived the same corridor, because they are trying to repay something that cannot really be repaid through the conventional mechanisms of repayment. Sprig's claim may be self-serving. It is also structurally believable. People who are helped by Disaster Inc. members tend to end up in the orbit doing things that are partly gratitude and partly the gravitational pull of unfinished business.

'Can I go now?'

Kaelor did not let him go. Kaelor searched him.

What he found was more important than the entire witness line combined.

Intercepted Pond Patrol communications.

The packet, as reconstructed from Kaelor's account and subsequent relay:

- Intercepted communications from the Pond Patrol concerning Raventree Manor.
- Language indicating active assessment of the manor as a target or objective — siege-posture phrasing, staging considerations, the vocabulary of organized movement toward a defended position.
- References to toad movements and rally points. The broader toad network — the Liberated Toads, the Pond Patrol, the organizational infrastructure that formed after the barrel discovery and solidified through repeated crisis — was now treating Raventree as a point of interest significant enough to generate formal communications about.
- Notes connecting the pyromancer hunt to the same area. Archie's trail, as always, leading toward the manor.
- A full transcript of the song We Are the Toads.

Waluigi is going to document the song transcript's presence in an intercepted intelligence packet because it is simultaneously the most absurd and most revealing detail in the recovery. A military or paramilitary intelligence packet containing a full song transcript means one of two things: either the song itself has operational significance — march timing, recognition codes, morale maintenance, rallying function — or the person who assembled the intercept was unable to distinguish operational content from cultural content and included everything. Either interpretation tells you something about the toads. If the song is operational, then toad logistics and toad musicality are not separate categories and have not been separate categories since the barrel toads came singing off the wrecked Vigilance. If the song is cultural noise accidentally included, then the line between toad operations and toad culture is blurry enough that an intelligence professional could not find it.

Waluigi suspects the former. We Are the Toads has appeared at too many operationally significant moments to be dismissed as background music.

Kaelor reached the same conclusion as everyone in this campaign eventually reaches: 'It seems like it all links back to Raventree.'

Sprig offered a lead: 'That green guy I was with might know.'

Kaelor did not let Sprig go anywhere alone. He forced Sprig back inside.

## Back Inside: The Goblins Escaped, the Room Is Empty, and Luigi Appears

The room had changed state.

The two goblin note-takers were gone. The door was open. Whatever structure the witness interview had possessed was now collapsed. The administrative pretense had evaporated the moment the hidden handler outside the window was exposed.

Luigi was there.

Waluigi has thoughts about Luigi being there and Waluigi is going to keep most of them to himself because Luigi's operational decisions deserve the respect of being assessed on their outcomes rather than their presentation, and the outcome is not yet known.

Luigi said he did not know Sprig the Mole.

Waluigi records the denial without endorsing or challenging it. Luigi often tells the truth in ways that sound like he is trying not to tell the full truth, and he also sometimes withholds entirely separate motives because he has, unlike some members of the wider orbit, retained a functional concept of privacy. Whether Luigi knew Sprig or not is less important, operationally, than what Luigi did next.

The questioning continued between Kaelor and Luigi. Both men had reasons to be suspicious. Both men had reasons to cooperate. The conversation moved from the cross-examination mode that had defined the witness interviews into something different: alignment.

Luigi explained that he and the rest of the people on the witness list had already agreed to sneak into Raventree Manor for Archie.

Waluigi needs to spend time on this because it reframes the entire witness line retroactively.

The witnesses were not merely people who knew something about Markop. They were, at least in part, people who were already planning to go to Raventree. The witness line was not only an intelligence-gathering exercise. It was a pre-formed expedition that happened to be using the interview process as its assembly point. Slick's debts. Ryan's search for his former group. Luigi's plan. The mage, the guard, the hammer bro — all of them apparently already committed to the Raventree operation before Kaelor walked in.

The office was not a briefing room. It was a staging area disguised as a claims office.

Luigi also had another reason for wanting to go in. He did not say what it was.

Waluigi could speculate. Waluigi will not here. A good archive distinguishes between inference and evidence.

What matters is that Luigi was not present incidentally. He was present on purpose, and his purpose was already pointed at the manor.

## The Departure: Everyone Except the Goomba

The session pivoted from investigation to mobilization.

The witness line became an expedition roster. The people who had come to offer testimony about Markop were now heading toward the place where Markop, Archie, and the entire Disaster Inc.-adjacent network appeared to be converging.

Everyone went except the goomba.

This is correct. The goomba brought newspaper clippings and a request to remove his shoes. The goomba contributed nothing the expedition needed. The goomba was last seen near the base of a window.

## Kaelor Judi Reveals His Name

By the end of the sequence, Markop's father formally identified himself.

Kaelor Judi.

Waluigi treats name revelation seriously in these records because names matter, especially near Raventree and especially near anything that has been touching the planar fracture. A father searching for his son began the session as a function: Markop's dad, the man with questions, the large skeptical force moving through lies with increasing impatience.

He ended it as Kaelor Judi.

That is a shift from role to person. The father becomes a named participant in the story rather than a named participant's unnamed relative. It also matters because the session began with a poster reducing his son to a bounty line — 'Markop Judi, crimes against magic, 2,000 gold' — and ended with Kaelor restoring human structure to the search by contributing his own identity to it. The poster offered a price. Kaelor offered a name.

## Assessment: How the Witness Line Became a Coalition

The goomba was a fraud.

Slick was part braggart, part genuine contact, and more useful than he first appeared.

Ryan remains one of the cleaner surviving links in the chain connecting Markop, Bones, the Vigilance, and the current dispersal.

Sprig the Mole is a facilitator, eavesdropper, and carrier of useful material whose motives may be partially sincere and are certainly incomplete.

Luigi is moving toward Raventree for Archie and for an additional reason he is not yet ready to disclose.

The Pond Patrol documents matter because they prove institutional or semi-institutional attention is now fixed on the manor.

The full transcript of We Are the Toads matters because, infuriatingly, even the most musical elements of toad logistics keep turning out to be real logistics.

Most importantly: Kaelor Judi now knows what Waluigi has been documenting from several angles already. Raventree Manor is where loose ends go when they stop being loose and start becoming structural.

This is how Disaster Inc.-adjacent coalitions form. Not by oath. Not by banner. Not by elegant mission briefing. By witness fraud, bruised stomachs, missing toads, unpaid debts, escaped goblins, a mole beneath a window, a wanted poster for your son, and the realization that if every bad road points to the same house, eventually you stop pretending there is a safer direction.

The team headed out.

WAH.

summary:
Waluigi was in a sauna for the middle third of this session and is going to address that directly because if he does not address it directly someone will address it indirectly and the indirect version will not contain the context that makes the sauna stay reasonable, which it was. The Feyward branch of Disaster Inc. operates under conditions where one wrong sentence binds your future firstborn to a butterfly court and one wrong silence lets a giant flower eat the building, and in that environment a hot spring is not a luxury, it is a tactical regeneration site.

The session began with Hjumpik attending a crisis planning meeting in the satyr encampment about how to deal with the Revel. Multiple proposals were raised: feed it beer until it explodes, feed it poison, feed it alcohol in massive quantities, cut the floor out from under it, feed it mushrooms, burn it. None of these proposals achieved consensus. A fairy named Kreetus Cetus estimated 455 kegs in the manor. A figure named Ratitus called the saw plan dumb. Arguments happened. Someone disappeared mid-conversation and Hjumpik stopped himself from questioning his own sanity. A brute satyr named Brutus challenged Hjumpik's authority, then split off with his own team and three conscripted fairies to pursue the mushroom plan. Hjumpik discovered a slim leather-bound volume in Woodfellow's library titled 'Concerning the Nature and Sustenance of Revels Eternal,' which warned that starving a Revel causes it to devour the revelers instead, and that the only true end is total surrender or someone willing to be remembered as the one who stopped the music. Hjumpik was given a library card by a goblin patron named Artameer Fellow. Outside, the goblin from earlier reappeared — having faked his disappearance — and proposed seducing the Revel with a flower. Hjumpik rejected this. The goblin began writing something down. Hjumpik chased him into Sedeia's chambers, grabbed him, found a single word written on paper: 'Brutus.' The goblin claimed it was dinner preparations. Hjumpik threatened him. The goblin stabbed Hjumpik with a pen that was actually a knife, then fled. Hjumpik chased him through the manor. The goblin, cornered, made the decision that defined his fate: he ran into the mushroom coat room and barricaded the door behind him, choosing the room full of recoiling parasitic mushrooms over the corridor with the angry dwarf. The mushrooms accepted the offer. By the time Hjumpik broke through, the goblin was on the floor, writhing, itching, fungal growths erupting through his clothing, fabric ripping, the boundary between goblin and mushroom dissolving in real time. Hjumpik brought the dying spored goblin to Sedeia. Sedeia attempted to replace the parasitic mushroom growth with a healing plant. The plant became a hundred-foot flower that crashed through the manor, generating overgrown plant life in a hundred-foot radius, which in a manor that is ALREADY the Overgrown Manor produced catastrophic compounding botanical chaos. The goblin's body became the seed-bed for the flower. Fire spread to the Lord's Chambers. The manor began evacuating upward. Shambling mounds spawned from the overgrowth. Sedeia was separated from Hjumpik when a door closed between them and a shambling mound. She reappeared later claiming to have defeated it, looking suspiciously uninjured. Hjumpik reached the upper mezzanine, found Lady Arulean playing piano with the heir, attempted to speak with her, was blocked by her guard Dave, shouted his name across the room, was ignored, received her response through Dave: the ritual table was covered in leaves and they had had to evacuate from it. Hjumpik entered the survivor's room — a moss-covered sanctuary with mushroom furniture and a forgotten tea set — and then found the sauna, where Waluigi was sitting in the hot spring on his Wahbook tablet reading about the previous session's events. Waluigi agreed to help. Waluigi changed. They returned to the Lord's Chambers. Waluigi summoned a localized ice storm. The fire was extinguished. The overgrowth was frozen. At least one person was dead. Hjumpik said that was perhaps too much. Waluigi said maybe. They cut through the frozen room. The session ended with the fire out, the ice in, the Revel consuming plant matter at an accelerating rate, and the structural situation of the manor significantly worse than it was at the beginning. Disaster Inc. continues to be present in the places it should never have entered, and continues to refuse to let the worst thing in the room remain unchallenged, and continues to make every situation it touches more complicated in the process.
description:
Waluigi is going to begin this entry by establishing a timeline, because this session's events overlap and compound in ways that require temporal clarity to reconstruct accurately, and because Waluigi was separated from Hjumpik for the middle portion and needs to document both tracks — what Hjumpik was doing while Waluigi was in the sauna, and what Waluigi was doing in the sauna while Hjumpik was being stabbed by a goblin who was about to make a decision that would end with the goblin becoming agricultural substrate.

The Feyward branch of Disaster Inc. — currently consisting of Waluigi, Hjumpik, and at various distances Wario, Rakasha, Azure, Sedeia, and whatever the Feyward decides to attach to the group on any given day — operates under the specific constraints that define every Feyward operation: every sentence is a tripwire, every bargain accumulates debt, every debt has flowers on it, and the architecture itself is participating. The manor is not a place where Disaster Inc. is having an adventure. The manor is a thing Disaster Inc. is in negotiation with. Sedeia's hundred-foot flower this session is a reminder that the negotiation can fail catastrophically when the participants do not understand what they are signing.

The timeline, as best Waluigi can reconstruct it from primary sources, Hjumpik's account, Sedeia's account (which Waluigi treats with measured skepticism for reasons documented below), and Waluigi's own direct experience of the portions he was present for:

Phase One: The crisis planning meeting. Hjumpik in the satyr encampment. Multiple proposals for dealing with the Revel. No consensus. The brute satyr splits off. Someone disappears. Hjumpik goes to the library.

Phase Two: Library research. Hjumpik finds the book about Revels. Receives a library card. Exits. Encounters the reappearing goblin. The goblin proposes seduction. Hjumpik rejects it. The goblin writes 'Brutus' on paper. Hjumpik confronts him. The goblin stabs Hjumpik with a pen-knife and flees. Chase through the manor. The goblin barricades himself in the mushroom room. The mushrooms accept him.

Phase Three: Sedeia's catastrophic plant replacement, using the dying spored goblin as the substrate. The hundred-foot flower. The overgrowth cascade. Fire in the Lord's Chambers. Shambling mounds. Evacuation. Sedeia separated from Hjumpik.

Phase Four: Hjumpik reaches the upper mezzanine. Attempts to contact Lady Arulean. Is ignored. Enters the survivor's room. Finds the sauna. Finds Waluigi.

Phase Five: Waluigi and Hjumpik return to the Lord's Chambers. Ice storm. Fire extinguished. Casualties.

Waluigi was present for Phases Four and Five directly. Waluigi's location during Phases One through Three was the sauna, which Waluigi entered after the party split documented in the previous session's entry and which Waluigi occupied continuously until Hjumpik arrived. Waluigi's activities during this period are documented below in the section addressing the sauna.

Waluigi proceeds with the full account.

## Phase One: The Crisis Meeting — Beer, Poison, Saws, Mushrooms, and the Fairy Who Could Count Kegs

The satyr encampment planning room. The same room documented in the previous session — vines everywhere, hammocks, worn beds, the accumulated detritus of people who have been living in a manor that is actively trying to become a forest. The planning group had assembled around the central problem: the Revel is eating everything, how do we make it stop.

Waluigi was not present for this meeting. Waluigi was in the sauna. What follows is reconstructed from Hjumpik's account and corroborated where possible by other sources.

The first proposal came from an unidentified participant: feed it beer so it blows up.

Waluigi wants to engage with this proposal analytically because it reveals assumptions about the Revel's biology that are worth documenting even though the proposal itself was not adopted. The assumption: the Revel, being a biological entity that consumes things, can be overloaded through consumption of a specific substance. The mechanism: the Revel eats beer, the beer does something inside the Revel that beer does not normally do inside biological entities, the Revel explodes. The reasoning gap: no evidence that the Revel processes consumed material the way organisms that can 'blow up' from overconsumption process material. The Revel eats and grows. That is what it does. Feeding it more of anything it can metabolize is feeding it more of anything it can metabolize. The proposal is, structurally, 'solve the eating problem by giving it more to eat.'

This is, in Waluigi's experience, a Disaster-Inc.-adjacent style of reasoning. Disaster Inc. has a long institutional history of solving problems by applying more of the thing the problem is made of. Archie's fireball inside the wooden airship is the canonical example. The Tea Party Incident was 'tension in a confined space, solved with combustion.' This room's first instinct — Revel that consumes things, solve by consumption — is the same cognitive shape. Waluigi notes the family resemblance even though the family member was not in the room.

Someone in the room identified this gap — 'no, it eats and grows power' — and redirected toward poison. If the Revel metabolizes what it eats, then feeding it something poisonous to Revels might damage it from inside. The candidate poison: alcohol. The argument: alcohol is poisonous. The counterargument: to what? Alcohol is poisonous to organisms with specific metabolic pathways. The Revel's metabolic pathways are unknown. It might be resistant. No one in the room knew.

The scale problem was also raised. A massive amount would be needed. Someone asked if there was a massive amount available. There was — the manor is stocked with wine and beer in quantities that would sustain a party of hundreds for an extended duration, because the manor HAS been sustaining a party of hundreds for an extended duration. But the Revel's tolerance was unknown, which meant the required dosage was unknown, which meant the 'massive amount' specification had no upper bound.

This is where the brute satyr — later identified as Brutus — asked the question that Waluigi considers the most operationally relevant question of the entire meeting, even though Brutus asked it with the energy of someone who was looking for a reason to dismiss the current speaker rather than with genuine analytical intent: 'What's your idea, Hjumpik?'

Hjumpik's response: the Revel isn't moving because it's being fed. If it stops being fed, it will move. If we don't feed it, it'll move or something.

This is the starvation hypothesis, and it is correct in its directional logic — a fed entity that is stationary because it is fed will become mobile when it is no longer fed — and catastrophically wrong in its practical implications, as the library book would later reveal. But Hjumpik did not have the library book yet. He was reasoning from available information, which did not include the specific warning that a starved Revel eats the revelers.

The response to the starvation hypothesis was also operationally correct: 'How do we stop feeding it? We're not the ones feeding it. Who's to say it doesn't wait too long and doesn't work?' The Revel is being fed by the ongoing party. Stopping the party requires stopping the satyrs. Stopping the satyrs requires either convincing them to stop or removing them. Neither option was available to the planning group in the room.

The saw plan: cut the floor. Cut around the Revel. Let it fall. This had been discussed in the previous session and was a persistent element of the planning. Ratitus — a new name in the documentation, a participant Waluigi has not encountered before — called it dumb. His reasoning: the floor will fall, the Revel will absorb the floor. The Revel absorbs what falls into it. Dropping the floor into the Revel is feeding the Revel floor.

Someone said Ratitus was drunk. Someone else said he wasn't. Arguments happened. The arguments escalated from the specific — is Ratitus drunk, is the saw plan dumb — to the general — who is in charge here, why are we listening to this person, what authority does anyone have. The brute satyr verbalized the general version: 'Why are we listening to some dwarf who's been barking orders?'

Hjumpik's response: 'We are both haters of the Revel. We can't question if we're together or not.'

This is diplomatic work. It is the specific diplomatic work of identifying the shared objective that holds a fractious coalition together and naming it before the fractures can become structural. 'We are both haters of the Revel' is the minimum viable coalition statement: we disagree about method, but we agree about the enemy, and that agreement is sufficient to keep us in the same room. The brute accepted it. Reluctantly, but he accepted it. This is the Disaster Inc. coalition-formation pattern operating at small scale. The party itself is not held together by belief. It is held together by shared enemies. Hjumpik replicated the pattern instinctively because the pattern works.

The compromise plan that emerged from the arguments:

- Half the group tries mushrooms. Feed them to the Revel. Maybe the mushrooms affect its biology in ways that alcohol wouldn't. Maybe mushrooms are toxic to Revels specifically.
- Someone suggested burning it. The burn faction was acknowledged.
- Brutus would take his own team. Hjumpik would take his. They would pursue parallel approaches.
- Brutus's team: find mushrooms, prepare to throw them into the Revel from above.
- Hjumpik's team: search around, find ideas, gather information.

Brutus walked out. He conscripted three fairies for his team by swiping them — physically grabbing them — which the fairies did not consent to and which no one present had the authority or inclination to prevent because Brutus was large and leaving and the fairies were small and in his hand. Hjumpik said 'Hey, wait a minute, I need a fairy' as they disappeared, but they were already gone.

Waluigi notes the fairy conscription because it establishes something about Brutus's operational style that matters for later events: Brutus takes what he needs without consultation and without concern for the preferences of what he takes. The fairies were afraid of him — the sources specify that the fairies were scared he might harvest them for power, which is a specific fear that implies either prior experience with being harvested or knowledge of what harvesters look like, and Brutus apparently looks like one.

The disappearance: someone in the room disappeared mid-conversation. Not left the room. Disappeared. The sources describe this with the flatness of an event that happened in front of witnesses and that the witnesses processed with the specific numbness of people who have seen too many strange things in this manor to generate surprise at one more. Hjumpik's internal response — 'Where did he go? Was he real?' — was immediately followed by self-correction: 'I won't question my sanity. Where did he go.'

Waluigi finds this self-correction significant. Hjumpik has reached the point in the Feyward experience where the impulse to question whether something was real is recognized as a trap — a cognitive trap that, once entered, has no exit, because in the Feyward the answer to 'was it real' is always 'it depends on what you mean by real and in the Feyward what you mean by real is not what you meant by real in the Material Plane and the Material Plane's definition of real is not available for consultation here.' Hjumpik refused to enter the trap. He reframed: not 'was it real' but 'where did it go.' The pragmatic question instead of the existential one. This is the correct cognitive strategy for Feyward operations and Waluigi approves of it.

Hjumpik later concluded that the person who disappeared was the same person who had known his name correctly — possibly a reference to Goblius Gobnilun from the previous session, though the identification is not confirmed in the sources. If the person who knew Hjumpik's name was the person who disappeared, then the pattern is: people who have accurate information about Hjumpik's identity do not stay in rooms for the full duration of conversations. They arrive with information, contribute it, and leave before their information sources can be examined. This is consistent with Waluigi's assessment from the previous session that Goblius's information was managed rather than organic.

## The Library: 'Concerning the Nature and Sustenance of Revels Eternal'

Hjumpik went to the library. His reasoning, which Waluigi reconstructs from the trajectory of his decisions rather than from explicit statement, was: the planning meeting produced proposals but not understanding. The proposals were based on guesses about the Revel's nature. The library might contain actual information about the Revel's nature. Actual information is better than guesses.

This is the correct reasoning. Waluigi has been advocating for this approach — consult the archive before committing to action — since the Feyward operations began, and Waluigi finds it professionally gratifying that Hjumpik independently arrived at the same conclusion, even if Hjumpik arrived at it by going to the library without Waluigi rather than by consulting Waluigi about going to the library.

The book was found in Woodfellow's library. Half-buried beneath a shelf that 'seemed to breathe when no one was looking,' which is the kind of detail that in any other setting Waluigi would flag as embellishment but in Woodfellow's library Waluigi treats as literal, because Woodfellow's shelves are extensions of Woodfellow and Woodfellow is a tree and trees breathe. The shelf was breathing. This is architecture, not metaphor.

The title: *Concerning the Nature and Sustenance of Revels Eternal.*

The binding: slim, leather-bound. The script: flowing, 'almost drunken,' shifting colors when read by firelight. The author: 'A Humble Participant Who Has Forgotten Their Own Name.'

Waluigi wants to document the author attribution because it matters. Someone who has forgotten their own name but remembers enough to write a coherent treatise on Revel biology is someone whose name was taken, not someone who lost it. In fey contexts, name loss is almost always transactional — you gave it away, it was taken, it was consumed. The author participated in a Revel, lost their name to it, and then wrote about the experience with the analytical clarity of someone who has been separated from their identity but not from their cognition. The treatise is a survivor document. The survivor survived without their name.

The content, as Hjumpik relayed it and as the sources document it:

The Revel is not an event. It is not a gathering. It is a living, hungry presence — 'a vast, many-limbed entity that slumbers in the spaces between songs and awakens when enough voices, enough wine, enough reckless joy is poured into the world.' This is the same characterization that the previous session established — the Revel is biological — but with specificity that the heir's disclosure lacked. The Revel is not merely biological. It is ecological. It exists in a relationship with its environment. It slumbers between songs and awakens when the songs are loud enough. The songs are fuel. The joy is fuel. The wine is fuel. Everything that constitutes a party — the noise, the consumption, the collective abandonment of restraint — is food.

The satyrs: never guests. Vessels. Their carousing is devotional feeding. They keep the Revel sated. They keep 'the manor's more dangerous hungers in check.' This is the first indication in the documentation that the Revel, for all its horror, might be serving a containment function — that the Revel being fed is preferable to whatever the manor's 'more dangerous hungers' would do if the Revel were not being fed. The Revel is the lesser evil. The party is the cage. The satyrs are the wardens who do not know they are wardens.

This aligns with Waluigi's standing theory about Raventree Manor across all its planar reflections: the manor is itself a participant, with appetites, with preferences, with a structural commitment to the destabilization of any identity that enters it. The Material manor attacks through mirrors and clothing. The Feyward manor attacks through hospitality and overgrowth. The mechanism is consistent across reflections even when the surface presentation changes. The Revel is one of the manor's organs.

The critical warning, in 'increasingly frantic marginalia': to starve a Revel is to invite it to devour the revelers instead.

This is the information that the planning meeting needed and did not have. The starvation hypothesis — Hjumpik's own proposal — is not merely ineffective. It is catastrophically dangerous. The Revel, when starved, does not shrink. It does not weaken. It redirects its hunger from the offerings to the offerers. The people at the party become the party. The distinction between the food and the fed collapses.

The only true end to a Revel, according to the text: total surrender, or 'the deliberate breaking of the circle by someone willing to be remembered as the one who stopped the music.'

Waluigi wants to analyze both options.

Total surrender: giving in. Letting the Revel consume everything. Accepting the Revel's dominion as permanent. This is not an ending — it is an abandonment of the project of ending. It is the option for people who have decided that fighting the Revel is worse than living inside it forever. Waluigi does not consider this an option, partly on principle and partly because Disaster Inc. has never once chosen surrender as a viable outcome and is unlikely to start now.

Deliberate breaking of the circle: someone stops the music. Someone is willing to be remembered as the person who stopped it. The phrasing is important — 'willing to be remembered.' Not 'willing to die.' Not 'willing to sacrifice.' Willing to be REMEMBERED. The cost is identity-based. You become, permanently and irreversibly, 'the one who stopped the music.' Your identity collapses into that single act. You are not a dwarf or a diplomat or a blacksmith after that. You are the person who ended the party. In a fey context, where identity IS power and names ARE selves, this is not a trivial cost. It is a different kind of death — the death of who you were, replaced by who you became in the moment of the breaking.

Hjumpik has this information now. The planning group does not. Hjumpik has not yet had the opportunity to share it with the planning group because the period between reading the book and the current moment has been filled with goblin espionage, a goblin spy becoming a mushroom, accidental botanical catastrophe, and fire.

The library card: Hjumpik received one. The patron who facilitated access was identified as Artameer Fellow — possibly the same Artameer whose card Wario stole in the previous session, or a different Artameer, or the same person under a slightly different name because names in the Feyward are unstable by nature. The card was given. Hjumpik asked to see the patron's card, the patron showed it, Hjumpik noted the name, the patron left. The interaction was transactional and efficient. Hjumpik now has library access. Woodfellow now recognizes Hjumpik as credentialed.

Hjumpik exited the library. What happened outside the library was significantly less organized than what happened inside it.

## The Goblin Spy: Flower Seduction, the Word 'Brutus,' the Pen-Knife, and the Decision to Run Into the Mushroom Room

Outside the library. Flower garden. Hjumpik pulling out a satyr — the sources are unclear on the context of 'pulling out a satyr' and Waluigi is not going to fabricate detail around it. The goblin from earlier appeared.

The goblin from earlier. Waluigi needs to identify this figure precisely because the session contains multiple goblins and the confusion between them has operational consequences. This is the goblin who disappeared from the planning meeting — the one Hjumpik thought might not have been real. He was real. He disappeared deliberately. He reappeared outside the library.

His explanation: 'I'm sorry, I had to put on a show for the cameras. People were watching. I had to smoke out of there.'

'Cameras.' 'A show.' 'Smoke out.' This is the language of someone who is performing for an audience that is not the people in the room. 'People were watching' does not mean the people at the planning meeting — they were the ones the goblin was performing FOR. 'People were watching' means someone else. An external observer. A patron. A handler. The goblin's presence in the planning room was intelligence gathering, and his departure was extraction, and both were conducted with the awareness that the operation had an audience.

The goblin's proposal: what if we seduce the Revel? He handed Hjumpik a flower.

Hjumpik rejected this immediately and correctly. 'Yeah no, that's a bad plan. We don't even know what it even is.'

The goblin said he would try it anyway. Later.

Hjumpik said he had a better plan. Asked: 'Goblin, can you be trusted?'

The goblin, while Hjumpik was formulating this question, was writing something down.

Hjumpik said: 'Hey, wait a minute.'

A chase. Into Sedeia's chambers. Hjumpik grabbed the goblin by the shoulder. A single word on the paper: BRUTUS.

Waluigi needs to document the significance of this because Hjumpik's reaction to it was immediate and aggressive and the reaction was correct.

Brutus is the brute satyr who split off from the planning meeting with three conscripted fairies to pursue the mushroom plan. Brutus's name, written on paper by a goblin who disappeared from the planning meeting and reappeared outside the library, is intelligence being transmitted. The goblin was documenting who was in the meeting, what they proposed, and who they were. The paper with 'Brutus' on it is either a report being prepared for delivery to someone, or a note for the goblin's own reference, but in either case it is the documentation of the planning group's composition by someone who was in the room specifically to document it.

The goblin's cover story: 'It's for the dinner preparations. Yes, he ordered quite a meal tonight.'

Hjumpik's response: 'I'm not a big fan of people who listen into others and give information they won't give.'

The ultimatum: shut your mouth about what happened earlier, or I stuff you in the Revel's mouth.

The goblin agreed. He handed Hjumpik his pen.

The pen was a knife.

Waluigi is going to spend time on this because the pen-knife is the detail that transforms the goblin from 'suspicious information gatherer' to 'actively hostile operative.' A pen that is also a knife is a weapon concealed as a tool of documentation. The goblin came to the planning meeting with a concealed weapon that was also the instrument he used to write down names. He documented the meeting's participants with the same object he was prepared to use on them. The dual function is not accidental. It is operational design.

The stabbing was not lethal — Hjumpik survived it and continued the chase — but it was committed. The goblin did not hesitate. The agreement to shut his mouth was a cover for the extraction of the weapon, which was a cover for the attack, which was a cover for the escape. Three layers of deception in the span of a sentence: agree, hand over the pen, stab, run.

Hjumpik chased him. The chase went through the manor — runs and blocks and a door that Hjumpik smashed through, which is the Hjumpik version of a locked door and which Waluigi has seen Hjumpik deploy enough times to consider it a standard entry technique rather than an improvisation. The goblin was faster in the corridors but Hjumpik was more committed and the manor's architecture — overgrown, tight, full of chokepoints — favored persistence over speed.

This is Hjumpik functioning as the endurance engine. Waluigi has documented elsewhere — at considerable length, in the Disaster Inc. structural overview — that Hjumpik is what the party becomes when persistence takes physical shape. Hjumpik makes retreat emotionally difficult because if Hjumpik is still advancing, everyone else feels shame at the thought of stopping. The goblin felt the pursuit pressure in the same way. He kept running because Hjumpik kept coming, and Hjumpik kept coming because Hjumpik does not stop. The chase was decided before it began. The goblin's only choice was where to be caught.

The goblin chose the mushroom coat room. He barricaded the door behind him.

## The Mushroom Room: The Goblin's Choice and the Body Hjumpik Found

Waluigi wants to be precise here because the previous reconstruction of this session — produced in haste, with incomplete information — described the mushroom room scenario as 'Hjumpik found a man on the floor with mushrooms growing out of him' and treated this man as distinct from the goblin spy. This was wrong. The man on the floor was the goblin. The goblin's decision to barricade himself into the mushroom room was a tactical decision about which threat he preferred to face. He chose the room over the dwarf. The room won.

Waluigi corrects the record. The corrected record:

The goblin spy, cornered by Hjumpik's pursuit, reached the mushroom coat room. He went inside. He barricaded the door behind him. The barricade was effective enough to slow Hjumpik. It was not effective enough to stop him. While Hjumpik worked through the barricade, the room did what the room does.

The room is the coat room that barely functions as storage because of the alarmingly huge mushrooms inside it. The mushrooms have sensory apparatus — they visibly recoil from light. They have responsiveness to their environment. They are not passive growths. They are organisms with awareness and reflexive behavior.

The goblin entered the room and barricaded himself with the mushrooms. This is a specific category of mistake. It is the mistake of a fugitive who has not considered that the room he is hiding in might be more dangerous than the pursuer he is hiding from. The goblin's threat model included Hjumpik. The goblin's threat model did not include the mushrooms.

Waluigi has thoughts about this. The goblin had been operating with apparent professionalism — concealed weapon disguised as documentation tool, intelligence gathering with extraction protocol, awareness of external observers — but he made a survival decision in a manor he was operating in as an outsider, and the survival decision was wrong because he did not know the manor as well as he thought he did. The mushroom room is not labeled. The mushrooms' behavior is not advertised. To know that this room would consume you, you would need to have either prior local knowledge or the kind of operational caution that includes not barricading yourself into unmarked rooms in foreign manors. The goblin had neither.

By the time Hjumpik broke through the barricade, the goblin was on the floor. Writhing. Itching. Mushrooms growing through his clothing. Fabric ripping as the growths expanded. He was alive — the writhing and itching confirm consciousness — but the mushrooms were consuming him from inside. The biological material that had been a goblin was becoming the biological material that would be mushrooms. The conversion was active. The boundary between the goblin and the fungus was dissolving in real time.

Waluigi notes the irony for the record because irony is documentation: the goblin who threatened to put Hjumpik in the Revel's mouth was being eaten by something else first. Hjumpik had said 'I will stuff you in the Revel's mouth.' The mushrooms stuffed the goblin into themselves. The threat structure inverted. The hunter became the substrate.

Whatever intelligence the goblin had been transmitting, whatever name 'Brutus' was being reported to, whatever operation he was part of — that information was now distributed across the cellular structure of a man being converted into fungus. The handler, if there was one, would not receive their report. The cameras the goblin had been performing for would not see the final scene. The goblin's operational career ended in a coat room.

Hjumpik picked up the body. The goblin was still alive in some technical sense. The conversion was not complete. There was still time, possibly, to separate the goblin from the mushrooms — if anyone in the manor had the capability to perform that kind of biological intervention.

Sedeia. Sedeia had the capability.

Hjumpik brought the goblin to Sedeia.

This was the humanitarian choice. It was also the choice that produced the hundred-foot flower. Waluigi does not fault the choice. Waluigi notes that the humanitarian impulse in the Feyward, applied without complete understanding of fey biological scale, tends to produce architectural-scale consequences.

## Sedeia's Mistake: The Hundred-Foot Flower and the Overgrown Manor Becoming MORE Overgrown

Sedeia attempted to replace the parasitic mushroom growth with a benign plant. The mechanism — plant substitution, fungal displacement, replacement of one biological system with another, using the dying goblin as the host substrate — is within Sedeia's documented capability range. What was not within her documented capability range was controlling the replacement plant's growth.

The plant became a flower. The flower grew. And grew. And grew. One hundred feet tall. Vines crashing through the manor's architecture. The structural walls — already compromised by the existing overgrowth that defines the Overgrown Manor's entire architectural identity — buckled under the additional botanical pressure. Chaos. Screams. People running.

The goblin's body. Waluigi wants to address this because the goblin's body was the seed-bed. The flower grew from the goblin. The hundred-foot flower has, as its root structure, the converted biological material of an intelligence operative who chose the wrong room to barricade himself in. The flower is, in a real biological sense, what the goblin became. Goblin to mushroom-substrate to flower. Three forms in approximately ten minutes. Whatever the goblin's handler eventually learns about his fate, the answer is that he is currently a hundred feet tall and on fire.

Waluigi needs to document the compounding effect because the compounding effect is what makes this a catastrophe rather than merely a problem.

The Feyward Manor is, by definition, the Overgrown Manor. Every inch of the building is covered in growth. Large sections have collapsed to accommodate huge trees. The wilds reclaimed this manor long ago. This is the baseline. This is what 'normal' looks like in this environment.

Sedeia's flower added a hundred-foot radius of thick, impassable overgrowth to an environment that was already overgrown. The game mechanic — four feet of movement for every one foot traveled — translates to a space where physical traversal has become nearly impossible. Corridors that were tight are now walls of vine. Rooms that were accessible are now sealed behind living plant matter. The manor's already-compromised structural integrity is further compromised by a growth event that treats the existing architecture as scaffolding for new biology.

Sedeia's response: 'It's a mistake. I didn't mean to.'

Waluigi believes her. Waluigi also notes that belief in the accident does not diminish the consequence of the accident, and that Sedeia's capability to cause this kind of event — even accidentally — establishes her as an entity whose interactions with the manor's biological systems need to be managed more carefully than they have been.

The flower bloomed. The bloom was the problem. Sedeia wanted to replace mushroom with flower. She got flower. She did not get flower at a manageable scale. The flower did what flowers do in fey environments — it grew to its full potential, and in a fey environment saturated with magical biological energy fed by the dying biological material of a magical creature, full potential is architectural-scale.

The overgrowth generated secondary effects: shambling mounds. The sources describe 'another ol' shambley' with the resigned familiarity of people who have encountered shambling mounds before in this manor and who have developed the specific weariness that comes from fighting the same kind of enemy often enough that it has a nickname. 'Shambley.' A shambling mound. A mass of animated plant matter given hostile purpose by the ambient magical energy of the overgrowth event.

One shambling mound pushed Hjumpik back. Another engaged Sedeia after a door closed between them, separating her from Hjumpik. Sedeia was left on the wrong side of the door with the shambling mound.

She reappeared later. She said she took care of the monster. She said it ran away.

Hjumpik sized her up. Couldn't tell if she was lying. Also noted: she didn't look hurt.

Waluigi's analysis: shambling mounds do not run away. Shambling mounds are animated plant matter without the cognitive architecture for tactical retreat. They advance, they grapple, they absorb. 'Running away' is not in their behavioral repertoire. Either Sedeia destroyed it — which would explain the lack of injury if the destruction was swift — or Sedeia did something else to it, or the shambling mound was never a genuine threat to Sedeia because Sedeia has a relationship with plant matter that shambling mounds cannot override.

The last option is the one Waluigi considers most probable. Sedeia accidentally grew a hundred-foot flower from a dying goblin. Sedeia's relationship with plant biology is not adversarial. If a shambling mound is animated plant matter and Sedeia controls plant matter, then Sedeia encountering a shambling mound is not a combat encounter. It is a management encounter. She told it to leave. It left.

She said it ran away because the truth — 'I told it to stop and it stopped because I am the reason it exists' — is a disclosure about the scale of her botanical control that she may not want to make, especially in the aftermath of accidentally creating a hundred-foot flower. Admitting you can control shambling mounds is admitting you operate on the same biological wavelength as shambling mounds, which is admitting you are part of the same system that just catastrophically destabilized the manor.

Sedeia did not look hurt because Sedeia was never in danger. The door closing between her and Hjumpik was, in Sedeia's experience, an inconvenience rather than a threat. Hjumpik's concern for her was genuine and also, from Sedeia's perspective, unnecessary.

Waluigi files this and continues.

## The Fire: The Lord's Chambers and the Evacuation Upward

The fire.

The Lord's Chambers — the opulent lounge turned feasting hall, the large firepit at the center, the roaring flame spewing smoke and embers — had always been a fire risk. The room's design — open flame, wooden tables, wine-soaked surfaces, everything covered in the organic material that defines every surface of the Overgrown Manor — was the design of a room that was waiting to burn. Sedeia's overgrowth event provided the accelerant. The giant plant's petals, leaves, and vines — pushed through walls and ceilings by the hundred-foot growth — made contact with the firepit's heat. Plant matter met flame. The Lord's Chambers caught fire.

The fire was not contained. The overgrowth that made traversal nearly impossible also made firefighting nearly impossible. The corridors were choked with vine. The routes to the Lord's Chambers were sealed behind plant walls. The treecutters — the organized resistance group that had formed in response to the overgrowth — were cutting, but the growth was faster than the cutting.

Two guards — one satyr, one goblin — assessed the situation outside the Lord's Chambers:

Guard one: 'Keep cutting the vines.'

Guard two: 'It's too big. If flower monsters come out, we need to take defensive positions. Maybe we will leave. Retreat.'

Guard one: 'But the Revel — if we leave it alone —'

Guard two: 'I know. I know.'

A third person approached. Not drunk — a rarity in the manor and a detail worth noting because sobriety in this environment implies either extreme discipline or recent arrival. The sober person delivered the critical intelligence update: 'The Revel is chewing on some plant leaves.'

Waluigi needs to stop here and address what this means.

The Revel is consuming the overgrowth. The giant flower's expansion — the hundred-foot radius of thick plant matter, generated from the body of an intelligence operative — has reached the Revel's feeding range. The Revel, which eats everything, is eating the new plants. The plants are food. The Revel is being fed by the consequences of the chase that ended in the mushroom room.

The causal chain, traced backward: the Revel is growing because it is eating the flower because the flower grew from the goblin because the goblin barricaded himself in the mushroom room because Hjumpik was chasing him because he stabbed Hjumpik with a pen-knife because he was caught writing 'Brutus' on paper because he was an intelligence operative for an unknown party in a manor where intelligence gathering is being conducted by parties whose identities and goals are not documented. The Revel's growth in this session is a downstream consequence of espionage that was directed at the planning group. The espionage produced the growth. The growth produced the food. The food produced the larger Revel.

The book said: a Revel that is fed grows. A Revel that is starved eats the revelers. The book did not address the specific scenario where a catastrophically overgrown plant system, generated from the body of an intelligence operative consumed by parasitic fungi, provides an effectively unlimited new food source. But the directional logic is clear: more food means more growth. The Revel is getting bigger because Sedeia's flower gave it more to eat.

The sober person said: 'It will grow and grow and...'

The sentence trailed off because the endpoint was obvious and terrible.

All three ran off.

Sedeia found Hjumpik. She said she screwed up. She said there was another shambling mound. She said there might be a stronger one. She said the plant monster was generating more monsters and they needed to cut it at the source.

Hjumpik patted her on the head.

Waluigi is going to document the head pat because it is the kind of detail that reveals character in ways that strategic analysis does not. The manor was on fire. The Revel was growing. Shambling mounds were spawning. The situation was, by any operational metric, deteriorating rapidly. Hjumpik patted Sedeia on the head and said: 'Let's go find the oracle.'

The head pat is not condescending in context. Sedeia is a plant creature. She is young, or presents as young. She made a mistake. The mistake was catastrophic. She knows it was catastrophic. She is standing in front of Hjumpik in the middle of the catastrophe she caused, telling him she screwed up, and she is — Waluigi infers from the tone of the account — scared. The head pat is: I hear you. The mistake happened. We are not going to stand here and process the mistake. We are going to go find the oracle. The pat is redirection through comfort, which is a diplomatic skill and also a parental skill and Hjumpik is deploying both simultaneously because the situation requires both simultaneously.

This is what Waluigi has elsewhere called the reflexive morality of Disaster Inc. The party does not build moral systems. They flinch toward the right thing when it becomes impossible not to see it. Sedeia is in pain. Hjumpik comforts her without breaking stride. The next problem requires attention. The comfort and the forward motion happen in the same gesture. This is not a planned ethical choice. It is the instinct of a person who has been in too many crises to separate care from action.

## The Survivor's Room: Moss, Mushroom Furniture, and the People Who Are Waiting to Die or Be Saved

Hjumpik entered the survivor's room. The only room in the manor not affected by the plants — because the room IS plants. The entire floor is moss and grass. Two small trees push against the ceiling. A stone bed has a mattress of living plants. Mushrooms large enough to sit on serve as furniture. A forgotten tea set with cups of clean water.

The room is sanctuary because the room is already what the overgrowth is trying to make the rest of the manor. 'How can we drink? Kegs are running low.'

The philosopher — a satyr's identity is tied to revelry, and the absence of revelry is the absence of self.

A beautiful woman walked in. A satyr noted her beauty. She walked into the closet.
