The discovery that he was more than he thought he was, followed immediately by the world's refusal to recognize what he had proved, is a combination that produces a specific kind of wound. The wound does not heal. It becomes the source of Mr. L, eventually  the alternate identity that refuses to suppress the capability Luigi proved he had. But in 963 BF, Mr. L has not yet emerged or has not yet been documented, and Luigi is still carrying the wound of 872 BF alongside ninety-one years of subsequent experience.

Luigi said '872? How do you even know about that?' He clutched his chest. He described the mansion as a complete catastrophe, the shadows moving even without light, the terror of thinking he would never see Mario again. He said everyone talks about it like a big heroic adventure but they were not the ones being chased through dark hallways by something with teeth. He mentioned that the Poltergust in 872 was a regular one, nothing that could pulse or explode like the Prototype-X. He said he was just trying to find his brother and survive the night.

'I was just trying to find my brother and survive the night.' Waluigi wants to hold this sentence because it is Luigi's complete mission statement in six words. Not glory. Not heroism. Not the defeat of evil or the rescue of kingdoms. Finding his brother. Surviving until morning. Everything else that happened in 872 BF was in service of those two objectives. And ninety-one years later, in the Long Dark, during the second year of civilizational infrastructure collapse, Luigi was still operating on exactly the same mission statement. Find the people you care about. Survive until morning. The scale of the crisis had expanded enormously. The objectives had not.

Luigi asked Leo not to talk about the past. The past was full of things that wanted to eat them. They should focus on getting to the train without meeting anything with teeth.

E. Gadd disagreed with this framing in the most E. Gadd possible way: he called Luigi a legend, cited the official archives, compared the 872 mansion to the Clockwork Spire and found the mansion wanting  'that was a simple haunting! A localized phenomenon!'  and expressed confidence that the Spire would be a much more scientifically interesting challenge. His enthusiasm for the relative complexity of the current threat was genuine. E. Gadd finds more interesting problems more enjoyable. The fact that more interesting problems are also more dangerous is not a consideration that appears to weigh heavily in his assessment.

## Part Three: The Station  Approximately the Thirteenth Hour and Thirty Minutes

They emerged from the tunnels into the Maglev Terminal Undercity's main concourse and Waluigi wants to describe this space in the detail it deserves because it is the clearest picture available of what Long Dark public infrastructure looked like from inside.

The station was massive. A cavernous hall of blackened iron and brass built into the hollowed-out underside of a significant geological structure, with gothic arches of dark soot-stained stone rising into a ceiling that was lost in actual darkness rather than atmospheric shadow  lost because the overhead lighting array that had once illuminated the full height of the space was running at approximately a third of capacity, leaving the upper reaches of the arches genuinely invisible from the floor. The architecture was still there. The scale was still there. The industrial grandeur of Guild engineering at its most ambitious was still structurally present in the bones of the building. It was just not visible, because the Long Dark had taken the light that would have shown it.

The blue mana-conduits that ran along the walls at mid-height were still fully operational, pulsing with Guild-maintained power, providing the primary illumination in the absence of the standard overhead lighting system. The Guild had prioritized these conduits because they served dual function as both lighting and infrastructure management systems for the platform operations below. They cast a cold blue light that made the station feel less like a transit hub and more like a space that had decided to keep operating despite the circumstances, which was an accurate characterization of what was happening.

There was no heating. The station's heating system had been among the first casualties of Long Dark power rationing  too large a draw on the emergency allocation to sustain, with too diffuse a benefit relative to the cost. The concourse ran at outside winter temperature, which in Chillwind in the Hoarfrost Winter season meant cold enough to see breath clearly, cold enough that exposed skin ached after extended periods, cold enough that the small coal braziers placed at intervals along the platforms were not merely a comfort measure but a genuine survival consideration for people waiting extended periods for services that might be delayed or cancelled. Travelers clustered near the braziers in shifting groups, moving away when they felt they had absorbed enough warmth to continue their business and returning when they needed more. This was how warmth worked in the Long Dark: not a constant ambient condition but a resource you moved toward and then moved away from, rationed by proximity and time.

The crowd was smaller than a pre-collapse transit hub crowd and more intense in a way that Waluigi has heard Long Dark survivors describe consistently. Everyone present had a specific reason to be there that justified the fuel cost of the service, the cold of the wait, the difficulty of the journey. No casual travelers. No one moving between locations for convenience or preference or curiosity. Every person in the station was there because being somewhere else was worse or because their business was urgent enough to qualify for Guild transit authorization. This produced a particular quality of presence  purposeful, watchful, not easily distracted  that was different from the varied and casual energy of a pre-collapse transit hub. The Long Dark had filtered the crowd down to people with serious intentions.

The line for the Iron Line platform stretched far into the gloom, winding around massive mana-conduits. Hooded scholars with scrolls. Armored mercenaries with weapons. Nervous apprentices carrying small enchanted lanterns  their own light sources, because in the Long Dark you carried light with you if you could. People in heavy cloaks clutching locked crates that could have contained almost anything but probably contained whatever was most valuable in the specific calculus of their particular emergency.

E. Gadd led them through with surprising vigor, eyes darting at every flickering lightbulb and puff of steam from the overhead pipes. He warned about missing the 14:05 departure. In the Long Dark, this was not a mild inconvenience warning. Missing the 14:05 meant the next Guild fuel allocation for this route was uncertain. The next service might be midnight. The next service might be days away if the Guild reassigned the fuel to a higher-priority route. The civilian settlement near the Spire was threatened now. The mission had a time component that was not flexible in the way that a standard transit delay would be flexible.

They reached the departures board. Platform Four. The Iron Line emergency service to the Foothills. E. Gadd admired the engines  the armored trains that were still running, the rolling fortresses that the Guild had kept operational when almost everything else had stopped, the physical evidence that some things were still working. 'Look at those magnificent engines! Truly a marvel of modern engineering!' he said, with genuine feeling, because E. Gadd's relationship with engineering achievements was the most uncomplicated positive relationship in his life.

Leo asked about boarding passes. E. Gadd produced the Guild Clearance Token from his lab coat pockets after extensive rummaging through vials and screws and a half-eaten biscuit that he quickly discarded. He held it up with the satisfaction of a man who has found exactly what he was looking for after being briefly worried he had misplaced it. The Token was a tarnished brass disc with the Magisterial Railway crest. He tapped it against a sensor. A gate swiveled open with a mechanical clunk.

In Chillwind 963, the Guild Clearance Token was worth something that it had not been worth pre-collapse. It was access to infrastructure. The difference between having it and not having it was not the difference between paying and not paying. It was the difference between being able to reach the Spire and being unable to leave the Guild District. The Token was one of the documents that made movement possible in a world where movement had become a resource rather than a default condition.

E. Gadd mentioned the heavy-duty scanners and the electromagnetic pulse verification. He said this as a procedural note, the kind of thing you mention when you are briefing someone on what to expect at a routine checkpoint. His tone did not suggest that the checkpoint was about to be a problem. This is relevant.

Luigi whispered 'scanners... electromagnetic pulses... heavy-duty security' in the tone of someone reading their own obituary aloud to make sure the grammar was correct. He suggested taking a carriage instead. A nice quiet horse-drawn carriage. He expressed concern that the more technology they used to get somewhere, the more likely something was to break and let a ghost inside. This is not as irrational as it sounds in the Long Dark context. Technology had been breaking and letting things in  cold, silence, darkness, disconnection  for fourteen months. Luigi's preference for simpler systems was evidence-based.

Leo identified the problem before anyone else did: 'Will the Poltergust on our backs affect it? This is a metal scanner right? This is already still sparking as it is.'

Waluigi is going to examine this moment carefully because it is the second significant data point in Leo's profile and it is important for the same reason the first one was. Leo had been wearing the Prototype-X for approximately thirty minutes. He had received no technical training beyond E. Gadd's verbal capability overview in the laboratory. He had heard one summary of the machine's capabilities and one summary of how it differed from standard units. And he identified the scanner interaction problem. Not because he was guessing. Not because the sparking made him vaguely worried about all possible consequences. Because he understood, from the explanation he had received, that the Prototype-X emitted electromagnetic flux as a byproduct of its operation, and that electromagnetic flux interacting with a high-intensity electromagnetic scanner would produce interference, and that interference could cause problems at the scanner threshold.

This is deductive reasoning applied correctly to new information. It is the kind of reasoning that produces correct predictions in novel situations. E. Gadd, who designed the Prototype-X and who knew about the checkpoint scanners, had not made this connection before the alarm sounded. Leo, who had heard about both for the first time thirty minutes ago, made the connection before reaching the checkpoint. The difference is not knowledge. E. Gadd had more knowledge of both systems. The difference is attentional focus. E. Gadd's attention was on the destination. Leo's attention was on the immediate environment and the implications of what was currently strapped to his back.

E. Gadd's response confirmed Leo was right: 'Great Galloping Ghost! You're right! The electromagnetic interference alone could scramble the sensor's logic gates!' He began pacing frantically. He described the potential feedback loop. He said 'Hullabaloo! Absolute hullabaloo!' He grabbed Leo by the shoulders with surprisingly strong hands for an old man and told him to engage the dampening shroud  a heavy lead-lined cloth in his side pocket  and wrap it tightly around the nozzle and the primary energy core.

Leo looked nervously at the people around them and expressed concern about reaching into his pocket in view of the security guards.

Luigi immediately understood why this was the right concern to have. He grabbed Leo's sleeve, pulled him toward the center of the walkway, and explained the optics problem with the specific clarity of someone who has thought about security checkpoints more than the average person because security checkpoints have historically been a point of friction in his professional experience. If the guards saw someone acting suspiciously  reaching into pockets in an unusual way near a security checkpoint  they might conclude contraband or attempt to disable security protocols. The guards had electrified stingers. The stingers would produce consequences before any explanation could be offered. Luigi told Leo to be quick, be smooth, to grab the shroud and wrap it up before hitting the sensor beam.

This is Luigi being operationally correct. Despite everything  despite hiding behind pillars and trembling and whispering funeral dirges about scanners  Luigi was accurately reading the security situation and providing good tactical guidance. His fear did not prevent his thinking. His thinking happened alongside his fear, in the same brain, at the same time. This is something Waluigi wants documented because the record on Luigi focuses heavily on the fear and lightly on the thinking, and this expedition demonstrates that both are consistently present.

Leo then asked how he had acquired the lead-lined cloth, because he did not remember packing it. E. Gadd explained with a wheezing cackle that it had been part of the standard-issue containment kit he had prepared, and that he must have slipped it into Leo's gear bag while Leo was examining the Prototype-X's intake valves, and that it was simply more efficient if Leo accepted that all necessary equipment had been pre-allocated by Gadd Science Inc. The scanner was already cycling. They were approaching the threshold.

This exchange is brief and revealing. E. Gadd put contingency equipment in Leo's bag without telling Leo. He did this because he had anticipated that the lead-lined cloth would be needed, because he had apparently anticipated that the Prototype-X might cause issues near the scanner, because he was the kind of person who prepares for the failure modes of his own plans without necessarily explaining that he is doing so. In the Long Dark, where resources were scarce and forgetting something could mean not having it, the habit of pre-allocating contingency equipment was more valuable than it appeared. It was also the habit of someone who did not fully trust that the people around him would think of everything themselves, and who had decided that the solution was to think of everything for everyone and distribute the results covertly. This is E. Gadd's operational style. It produces results. It also produces situations like the current one, where the person carrying the contingency equipment was not informed of its existence or purpose until the contingency became necessary.

## Part Four: The Checkpoint Incident  Every Moment

Waluigi is going to document the checkpoint incident in full, moment by moment, because it contains the highest density of behaviorally significant data in the entire departure sequence. Every person reveals something essential about themselves in this four-minute window. Every choice made and not made matters. Waluigi wants none of it summarized.

The scanner began cycling. Low-frequency hum that Waluigi's sources describe as felt in the sternum before it was heard with the ears. A rhythmic pulsing blue light from the scanner array that made the air around the checkpoint feel slightly different in quality, slightly charged. The group was walking toward it.

They stepped under the first archway.

A violent crackle of blue electricity jumped from the sensor to the metal floor. This is the security anomaly report's description: violent crackle, immediate arc to ground, suggesting significant electromagnetic surge rather than normal activation. A piercing siren began to wail. A bright red light started rotating atop the gate. Guards in the distance turned at the noise.

E. Gadd: 'CRIMINY! The interference is spiking! It's sensing something! Quick, get that shroud moving! The guards are turning around!'

Heavy boots. Electrified batons crackling. Two Guild guards who had been at the scanner perimeter began jogging toward the source of the alert.

Luigi fell apart. Waluigi says this descriptively rather than critically. Luigi went into full panic response: 'They're coming! They're definitely coming! Oh no, oh no, oh no... I knew it! We're going to get arrested in the middle of a crowded station!' This is Luigi's nervous system registering maximum threat and producing maximum response. It is physiologically appropriate. It is operationally counterproductive in the precise moment in which it occurs. Luigi knew this, which is part of why his own panic upset him even as he was experiencing it.

Leo's first attempt to address the problem was direct and physical. He fumbled into his pocket, found the cold heavy strangely textured lead-lined fabric, yanked it out, and tried to drape it over the glowing pulsating nozzle.

He missed.

Waluigi needs to spend a moment on the failure before describing the consequence because the failure is not evidence of incompetence and should not be read as such. Leo had been wearing the Prototype-X for approximately forty minutes total. He had never handled the machine before that day. The dampening shroud was a component he had been told existed approximately five minutes before being told to use it, under scanner alarm conditions, with guards approaching. He was trying to cover a component attached to his back  working blind, reaching behind himself, unable to see what he was doing. The miss was predictable. It was the predictable outcome of insufficient training time on equipment physical layout, which was E. Gadd's planning failure rather than Leo's operational failure.

The consequences of the miss were severe. The cloth snagged on one of the Poltergust's protruding brass valves. As Leo pulled trying to free it, he inadvertently dragged the entire vacuum unit toward the scanner's sensor beam. The increased proximity to the beam produced a catastrophic interaction: a deafening metallic crack, a bolt of blue electricity leaping from the scanner directly into the Poltergust's nozzle, and then the machine's polarity reversed. Instead of suction inward, it began generating rhythmic bursts of pressurized glowing green sparks outward from the nozzle in an energetic and highly visible display.

Luigi produced a sound at a pitch that nearly matched the station siren and fell backward, scrambling on his hands and knees across the metal grating, getting as far from the sparking machine as the available space allowed: 'IT'S REVERSING! THE VACUUM IS REVERSING! IT'S GOING TO BLOW! WE'RE ALL GOING TO BE SUCKED INTO ANOTHER DIMENSION!'

Leo: 'Shut up Luigi, guards will hear us! Do something Egadd please!'

Luigi clamped both hands over his mouth. The sound this produced was a series of muffled whimpers and a hiccup. He retreated to crouch behind a nearby luggage trolley, peering around it with one eye visible, looking exactly like a person who is aware that hiding behind luggage trolleys is not a high-quality tactical position but has chosen it anyway because it is the best option currently available.

Leo looked to E. Gadd and found him frozen in place.

Waluigi wants to note this honestly because E. Gadd's field notes are honest about it: there was a moment of complete paralysis. The guards were within meters. The machine was sparking visibly and dramatically. A large burst of green sparks had just struck a nearby metal trash bin with a loud clang that had drawn additional attention from the vicinity. The scanner's siren was still sounding. And E. Gadd was standing very still, his face pale, his eyes darting between the approaching guards and the sparking Poltergust on Leo's back, in the manner of someone whose system had briefly exceeded its processing capacity and was rerouting.

Then his expression changed. The paralysis became calculation. The wide-eyed panic became focused attention directed at the station's infrastructure rather than at the guards or the equipment. His gaze fixed on a large overhead steam pipe running directly above the security checkpoint  dripping with condensation, pulsing with high-pressure heat. His hand moved into his lab coat pocket.

E. Gadd stepped forward. He placed himself between Leo and the lead guard with the bearing of a man who has never in his life been intimidated by authority and has no intention of starting now. He adopted exaggerated academic politeness  a tone so specifically professorial that it created a small zone of expected deference around him, the social assumption that someone speaking in that register was either important or had a very good explanation ready and was about to deliver it. He waved dismissively at the guard's scanning device. He talked about humidity and condensation clogging intake sensors. He talked about the atmospheric volatility of the station. He expressed concern that such fine Guild equipment might be ruined by misplaced suspicion.

He pulled a small glass vial of swirling neon-blue liquid from his lab coat. He held it up to the overhead light so it caught and refracted in a visually interesting way. He said he was just about to deploy it to calm the static friction in the area.

His thumb pressed a button on the side of the vial.

The vial was not atmospheric stabilizer. The button triggered a remote release valve that E. Gadd had identified on the overhead steam pipe during his pre-checkpoint assessment of the station's infrastructure. He had noted which pipes still had operational pressure in the Long Dark  not all of them did, since many steam systems had been shut down as part of power rationing  and he had identified this pipe as a potential distraction asset before the alarm ever sounded. He had then put a remote trigger in his pocket as part of the standard-issue contingency kit that he had prepared and distributed without telling anyone he was preparing and distributing it.

A sudden loud hiss from the overhead steam pipe. A thick blinding cloud of white steam billowed downward, rapidly obscuring the scanner, the guards, the luggage trolley, and most of the immediate checkpoint area. The steam smelled of hot metal and damp concrete and the particular industrial quality of station infrastructure heated past its comfort point.

E. Gadd, barely audible through the roar: 'Quickly! The distraction won't last! The secondary alarm will trigger once the visibility drops below safety standards! You have to make your choice  the purge or the retreat! Go, go, go!'

Leo chose purge. And he chose to do it slowly.

This is the decision that Waluigi finds most analytically significant in the entire checkpoint incident. The temptation in that moment  steam cloud, guards confused, time pressure, machine still sparking  was to do the purge as fast as possible and get out. Maximum speed. Maximum noise. Maximum chance of detection, because a full release would sound like a cannon blast and the guards were still within earshot. Leo chose instead to execute the purge at minimum viable speed to minimize the acoustic signature, accepting the extended time pressure and the extended physical discomfort of holding a lead-lined cloth against a machine building toward pressurized release, because the quieter approach had better odds even if it felt less urgent.

This is risk assessment under pressure. The faster option felt safer because it was faster. The slower option was actually safer because it was quieter. Leo correctly identified this distinction and acted on the correct assessment rather than the emotionally compelling one. This is the kind of judgment that saves lives in field operations and that is extraordinarily difficult to fake or perform without genuine internalized understanding of the relevant tradeoffs.

Leo began sliding the FLUX PURGE toggle with agonizing slowness. The Poltergust gave a low rhythmic throb. The lead-lined cloth bulged outward as pressure built under it. Heat radiated through the fabric, scorching his palms. A tiny hiss escaped  barely audible, no louder than a slow leak in a bicycle tire.

E. Gadd murmured beside him: 'Steady... steady hands... like a surgeon dissecting a Boo...'

The guard's scanner  visible faintly through the mist  shifted from solid angry crimson to hesitant pulsing amber. The purge was working. The energy was bleeding off into the lead lining. The detectable electromagnetic signature was dropping.

Then a guard swung his baton blindly through the steam. It struck a metal railing. The crack was much louder than the purge had been. 'I heard something!' The heavy boots were no longer wandering randomly  they were charging directly toward the source of the residual vibration from the Prototype-X's operation.

Leo made his final decision in the remaining seconds available.

He wrenched the FLUX PURGE toggle from the controlled slow position to full release. The silver toggle snapped into the Full Release position with a definitive click. A massive concussive blast of green energy erupted from beneath the lead-lined cloth  not a sound exactly but a physical event, a pressurized thud that sent a shockwave through the metal flooring and rippled the thick steam cloud like a stone thrown into water. An emerald flash illuminated the entire checkpoint area for a split second through the mist, bright enough to be visible from some distance away.

In the exact millisecond the blast hit:

'AAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHHHH! MY TOE! I STEPPED ON A SHARP COIN! OH, THE AGONY! THE UNBEARABLE HUMAN SUFFERING!'

Waluigi wants to give the scream the analysis it deserves, because the scream was not a panic response. The scream was a calculated professional tool deployed with complete commitment.

Leo had identified several things simultaneously. He had identified that the purge would produce a noise and a light event that would require explanation. He had identified that the explanation needed to be human-scale and emotionally compelling rather than technical, because the guards were not engineers assessing electromagnetic phenomena  they were security personnel responding to a disturbance, and security personnel responding to a disturbance are susceptible to a sufficiently convincing human emergency. He had identified that the timing needed to be perfect  the scream had to begin at exactly the moment the blast occurred to mask the blast's sound within the scream's duration. And he had identified that the content of the scream needed to be specific enough to be believable but trivial enough to be funny, because funny is disarming and disarming is the operational goal.

A coin. A toe. The unbearable human suffering of a minor foot injury. Not vague pain  a specific, identifiable, completely non-threatening cause. Something that explained the sudden sound and movement without implicating spectral equipment or unauthorized energy discharges. Something that made the guards falter not just from confusion but from the very human response to witnessing what appeared to be genuine physical suffering in a stranger.

The execution was total. Leo committed to the performance with everything available to him. The scream was visceral, theatrical, continuous, exactly loud enough to cover the blast, exactly emotional enough to be credible. E. Gadd, who witnessed it, was momentarily stunned before his assessment capabilities caught up and he immediately began his supporting performance: 'CRIMINY! A medical emergency! A catastrophic toe-related incident! It's a localized tremor caused by extreme physiological distress!'

The lead guard skidded to a halt. Through the swirling white mist, the glow of his visor. He looked at Leo's hunched form, the smoking machine on Leo's back, his own partner. He said to his partner: 'Did... did that kid just scream because of a coin?'

Behind him, the second guard's scanner: steady, unremarkable green. No abnormal energy readings detected in the immediate vicinity. The purge was complete. The Prototype-X was reading clean.

E. Gadd's field notes contain one sentence about the scream. The sentence is: 'The trainee's improvisation during the scanner incident exceeded expectations considerably.' Waluigi has read thousands of pages of E. Gadd's field notes across multiple years of documentation. E. Gadd uses the word 'considerably' approximately once per fifty pages. He uses it to describe things that genuinely surprised him, things that produced results beyond what his models predicted. The scream exceeded his expectations considerably. This is high praise from a man who does not give high praise in those specific words without meaning it precisely.

## Part Five: The Newsstand, the Map, and the Bypass Plan  Approximately the Fourteenth Hour

The checkpoint incident was resolved but the checkpoint was now watched by guards who were confused rather than convinced, which was an improvement but not a comfortable position to maintain. E. Gadd immediately redirected toward a cluttered newsstand near the platform edge, pulling Leo into the shadow behind a stack of oversized vibrating newspapers advertising 'The Latest Spells for Home Security.'

The newsstand vendor  a small hunched creature with four eyes who Waluigi's sources describe as appearing entirely preoccupied with a glowing ledger  did not look up at the arrival of three people who had just caused a station alarm. This is consistent with what Waluigi has observed about Long Dark-era vendors at transit hubs: their primary economic function had shifted from retail to information management, and they had developed a professional incuriosity about anything that was not directly relevant to their ledgers. The newsstand operated. The vendor operated. The three people hiding behind the newspapers were not their problem.

Leo picked up a newspaper from the stack. The Mushroom Chronicle. The paper felt unnervingly cold and damp against his hands. The ink crawled slightly on the page  a self-contained magical enchantment designed to keep the text current, one of the few magical conveniences still functioning during the Long Dark because it was wholly self-contained rather than dependent on the Star Road network. Whatever energy the crawling-ink enchantment used, it carried within the paper itself, renewing each page's content through some mechanism Waluigi does not fully understand but which clearly worked independently of external infrastructure because it still worked fourteen months after the infrastructure had failed.

Leo found an article about a recent shortage of Star Bits. He stared at the lines of text, tracking them with his eyes, while keeping his attention split toward E. Gadd's face visible through the gaps in the newspaper.

Waluigi needs to address the Star Bit shortage article specifically because calling it a shortage is the kind of institutional language that deserves direct examination. The Star Road Network was destroyed in 962 BF. The Star Fountains that produced Star Bits  crystallized fragments of celestial energy harvested from the Star Road  had been operating at dramatically reduced output since before the network's destruction and had been producing approximately four percent of pre-collapse baseline for the past several months. Four percent. This was not a shortage in any meaningful economic sense of the word. A shortage is a temporary imbalance between supply and demand. What the Mushroom Kingdom had in Chillwind 963 was closer to near-total cessation of a currency's fundamental supply mechanism. The Mushroom Chronicle calling this a shortage was either deliberate euphemism, designed to avoid the panic that accurate language might produce, or evidence that the publication's editorial standards had been calibrated to pre-collapse conditions and had not fully adjusted to the reality of what post-collapse language needed to say.

Leo was reading an article that described civilizational economic collapse in the vocabulary of a supply chain inconvenience. He was doing this while standing in a cold station with an experimental machine on his back that had just set off a scanner alarm that he had resolved by screaming about a coin. This was the world in Chillwind 963. You read about the end of your civilization's monetary system in a newspaper that described it with the same tone as a temporary sugar shortage, and then you got on the train.

E. Gadd spread his hand-drawn map of the station's subterranean service tunnels on a crate of mana-batteries. The map was a chaotic web of glowing lines and scribbled notations  the station's official layout overlaid with E. Gadd's personal additions, which consisted of dashed red lines representing service passages, junction markings for key decision points, and small symbols Waluigi cannot fully decode but which appear to represent hazard types based on the context of where they appear. The map was not something E. Gadd had made for this expedition specifically. This was a pre-existing document. E. Gadd had this map already.

He described the bypass plan: the secondary ventilation shaft below Platform Four, winding through narrow cramped corridors that bypassed the main scanner array entirely. The shaft was narrow, dusty, smelled like a wet Polterpup, and was being serviced by automated cleaning golems that would detect and attempt to remove unauthorized organic matter. To pass through the shaft, they would need to disable the golems' sensors using the Poltergust's suction without triggering station-wide lockdown. No screaming. No exploding vacuum cleaners. No spontaneous theatrical performances. He said this last point looking at Leo with specific emphasis.

Five minutes before the departure. They needed to move now.

Leo asked Luigi if the maintenance ducts were similar to warp pipes.

E. Gadd's response was approximately ninety seconds in duration and consisted of a detailed, indignant, and technically accurate comparison between warp pipes and industrial ventilation systems. He noted that warp pipes were controlled environments, predictable, providing smooth transit through emerald-green corridors with a sense of joyful momentum. He noted that these maintenance ducts were filled with soot, rusted iron, discarded magical scraps, and unpredictable cleaning golems, and that one wrong move would result in the operator being compressed into a small, unidentifiable cube of organic matter. He compared the experience to crawling through the digestive tract of a very old, very angry iron dragon. He said they needed to be precise, quiet, and above all invisible.

Leo's response: 'Alright let's go.'

Two words. The ninety-second comparison received two words. The information was received, processed, and converted into readiness to act in approximately the time it takes to say 'alright' and 'let's' and 'go.' Waluigi keeps returning to Leo's response times because they are consistently shorter than expected for someone receiving complex, high-stakes information for the first time. The processing is fast. The commitment follows the processing immediately. There is no visible interval of hesitation between understanding and willingness to proceed. This is either trained behavior or natural temperament, and either way it is not what first field deployment trainees typically demonstrate.

## Part Six: The Maintenance Tunnel  Every Detail

They slipped away from the newsstand under the cover of an incoming train's arrival noise. A massive iron locomotive screeching to a halt provided exactly the kind of broad acoustic signature that masked the sound of three people moving quickly through a crowd toward a maintenance hatch. E. Gadd reached the hatch first  heavy rusted iron door, a small glowing keycard that he fumbled with for several seconds before the latch disengaged with a sickeningly loud clang that seemed much too loud given everything, though nobody in the distracted station crowd appeared to notice.

A gust of stale freezing air hit Leo in the face as the door cracked open. Old oil smell. Something metallic that had the quality of dried metal rather than fresh, the smell of a space that had not been properly ventilated for an extended period. Interior: pitch black beyond the door's threshold, visible only as a void into which the station's dim blue light did not reach.

Leo ducked in and asked: 'This is just to cut the line right? Since you said we have seats, where do we exit?'

This question is, on its surface, a simple request for navigation information. Waluigi reads it as something more: Leo was verifying that the plan had two halves. He had been told where they were going. He was confirming that there was a path out as well as in. In the Long Dark, in a maintenance tunnel system beneath a transit hub, this is not a trivial concern. If the exit was unclear or contested or not where E. Gadd expected it to be, knowing that before going deep into the tunnel was operationally critical. Leo asked the question that needed to be asked before they were committed to the tunnel's interior.

The tunnel was narrow enough that their shoulders brushed against the metal walls with almost every movement. The floor was uneven and covered in a layer of slick oily sludge  hydraulic fluid residue, cleaning solution runoff, the accumulated moisture of ventilation ducts that had been processing the station's air for decades. E. Gadd's handheld lantern, a dim sickly yellow, illuminated approximately four feet of the passage ahead at any given time. The walls were lined with thick pulsating cables that looked disturbingly like giant copper worms  active conduits still carrying Guild power through the station's infrastructure, warm to the touch if you made contact with them, humming with a frequency that was felt before it was heard.

E. Gadd explained the exit plan: follow the secondary conduit to the sublevel maintenance hub, emerge near the station's lower freight terminal, far enough from the main security scanners to regroup safely. Then:

A loud mechanical thud from deeper in the tunnel. A rhythmic grinding sound  heavy metal limbs moving against stone. The cleaning golem was already on patrol in this sector.

Waluigi needs to spend a paragraph on the golem's condition in the Long Dark context because the condition matters to everything that follows. The Maglev Terminal's cleaning golems ran on the station's clockwork systems, which in turn ran on the same power allocation that ran everything else in the Long Dark  reduced, rationed, operating at a fraction of pre-collapse capacity. In practical terms this meant the golem's patrol cycle was slower than its designed speed. Its optical sensor recalibration time after sudden light changes was longer than designed. Its threat assessment processing  the computation that determined whether a detected organic presence was authorized or unauthorized  was running on degraded power, which produced response times slightly longer than specifications.

This was still a multi-ton armored construct with active programming to compress unauthorized organic matter. Its being degraded did not make it safe. It made it slower in specific ways, and those specific ways created windows that a fast and accurate operator could exploit. The Long Dark had weakened the obstacle along with everything else it had weakened, and this was the first time in this account that the Long Dark's damage worked in the team's favor rather than against them.

E. Gadd held the lantern low. In the distance through the gloom: a rhythmic sweeping of bright clinical white light passing across the walls. The golem's scanning beam. He breathed: 'The cleaning golem... it's already on patrol in this sector! Keep your head down and stay close to the wall! If that light hits us, we're finished!'

Leo pressed his back against the tunnel wall and reached for the Poltergust. He told E. Gadd he would stick close and prepare to disable the golem stealthily. He looked to Luigi and signaled for him to take position  a firm silent nod, the specific gesture of someone who has given tactical positioning commands before even if they have never done so in this precise context.

The golem emerged from the darkness fully as they watched. Massive. Hulking. Multi-limbed brass and white porcelain construction moving with an unnerving jerky precision, each limb articulating in carefully calibrated sequence that made it seem simultaneously mechanical and organic. The scanning beam  brilliant sterile white  swept across the tunnel floor, illuminating the oily sludge, passing just above Leo's feet before moving on. The golem's eye  a single rotating lens in the center of its porcelain face  spun rapidly as it scanned the corridor.

The golem stopped. The grinding ceased. In its place: a low-frequency hum that made teeth ache and created a slight pressure sensation in the inner ears. Its mechanical limbs twitched, testing the air for vibration, for heat differential, for any of the signatures that unauthorized organic presence would produce. A small sensor appendage extended from its central chassis, sniffing at the darkness in the specific way that machines sniff when they are trying to confirm what their primary sensors have suggested.

The scanning beam began swinging back toward Leo's position. Faster this time  the golem had detected something and was concentrating its search.

Leo had calculated his approach: not full-power suction, which would be too loud and too obvious, but a concentrated burst of light-refraction from the Prototype-X's internal spectral flare, targeted at the golem's rotating lens to overload its optical sensors. The flare would not need to be silent  the station above them was producing enough ambient noise to cover a brief flash  but it needed to be precisely aimed to hit the lens rather than scatter generally, because scattered refraction might affect the golem's other sensors without disabling the optical one, which would produce a confused and still-active threat rather than a temporarily blind one.

Leo waited. The beam swept across his face. He squinted against the light. He held his breath until his lungs ached. The golem paused directly above his position. The mechanical gears clicking in its translucent neck joints were audible in the relative silence.

He squeezed the trigger.

VROOOOM-FLASH.

A sudden violent burst of brilliant prismatic light erupted from the Prototype-X nozzle, hitting the golem's lens dead-on. The vacuum's spectral flare caught the sterile white light and scattered it into a blinding kaleidoscopic explosion within the narrow tunnel  every surface, every wire, every oil-slicked patch of floor suddenly lit in every color simultaneously, too much visual input for any optical sensor to process into meaningful data.

The golem let out a high-pitched electronic screech of pure mechanical confusion. Its limbs flailed wildly, clanging against the tunnel walls with deafening force. It staggered backward on the oily sludge, its heavily calibrated footfalls losing their precision as the optical feedback overloaded its balance systems.

E. Gadd from the alcove, barely able to contain his scientific excitement despite the circumstances: 'It's working! Keep going!'

But as the golem staggered backward, it slammed into a junction box mounted on the tunnel wall. Sparks showered down like dying stars, hissing and crackling against the floor and walls. The impact caused a section of the tunnel to shudder violently. And the golem's eye  which had gone white-blind from the spectral flare  began flickering erratically. White to red. Unstable red. And then: steady, pulsing, hunting red. The golem was switching from optical detection to thermal and motion tracking. It was recalibrating.

A fully powered pre-Long Dark golem would have made this switch in approximately one second. The Long Dark degradation extended this to approximately four or five seconds  still very fast, but fast in a way that created a window. Four or five seconds during which the golem's sensors were in transition, its processing capacity split between managing the residual feedback from the optical overload and activating the thermal systems, its attention divided.

Leo: 'Luigi now take it down, I got its eye!'

Luigi's response: 'Take it down?! Take it down?! It's a multi-ton armored construct, not a common Boo! It has reinforced plating!'

Luigi scrambled deeper into the copper cables. He claimed afterward in the debrief that he had been preparing an electromagnetic pulse grenade  a small device on his belt designed to create a localized EMP that would shut down the golem's electronic systems entirely. Waluigi has assessed this claim and believes it is accurate. Luigi had the grenade. He had the expertise to deploy it correctly. The EMP approach would have worked. It would also have taken approximately eight to twelve seconds to prepare the detonation sequence, produced a larger electromagnetic signature than Leo's approach, and risked triggering the station's secondary electromagnetic monitoring systems that were already sensitized from the checkpoint incident. Luigi's approach was valid in principle. Leo's approach was better in practice given the specific constraints of the situation. Both things are true simultaneously, and Luigi's wounded professional pride afterward was both understandable and slightly unfair to the situation.

Leo did not wait for Luigi to finish expressing his alarm. He moved.

He slid forward on the slick oily floor with the controlled motion of someone who had calculated that running would create too much vibration but that stillness would give the recalibrating golem time to lock on. The slide was a specific choice: fast enough to cover distance, quiet enough to not produce the acoustic signature that would accelerate the golem's threat assessment. The golem was still focused on the junction box it had slammed into, its red eye flickering as it processed the electrical interference from the sparks. This was the window.

Leo identified the hydraulic pressure intake vent on the side of the golem's neck  a small recessed opening, perhaps two inches across, where the hydraulic fluid that powered the golem's limb articulation circulated from the central reservoir to the peripheral actuators. He identified this in darkness, under active threat, on a machine he had never encountered before. He aimed the Prototype-X nozzle directly at the vent opening. He flicked the activation switch to Pulse Mode  rapid-fire high-frequency suction bursts rather than continuous suction  because the hydraulic valve would respond better to repeated sharp pulls than to sustained suction pressure.

THWIP-THWIP-THWIP.

The nozzle clamped onto the intake valve edge. The suction bursts hit the valve plate in rapid sequence. Heavy resistance  the valve plate was designed to stay in place under pressure, sealed against exactly this kind of failure mode. And then a sickening POP as the valve plate sheared from its housing under forces it was not engineered to withstand from this direction.

Pressurized blue hydraulic fluid sprayed outward from the ruptured housing in a fan pattern, coating the tunnel walls and ceiling and floor and Leo and the nearest surfaces of the golem itself in a thick glowing mist. The golem's internal hum  which had been a steady operational drone through the whole engagement  shifted instantly to a frantic dying wheeze as the hydraulic pressure driving its limb actuators dropped toward zero. The red light in its eye sputtered three times. Turned dim and sickly. Faded entirely to darkness.

The massive construct sagged. Then the limbs lost their tension entirely and it collapsed  not a controlled shutdown but a complete structural failure, the kind that produces a bone-shaking concussive CRUNCH as several tons of brass and porcelain hit the floor simultaneously. The silence that followed was the silence of something that was running until it suddenly was not.

Only the rhythmic dripping of hydraulic fluid onto the tunnel floor.

E. Gadd peeked out from behind the copper cables. His face was pale, covered in a thin layer of dust from the collapse's impact, his spectacles skewed sideways on his face. He looked at the slumped machine. He looked at Leo. He breathed: 'You... you actually did it... You bypassed the entire logic core with a single suction burst... That was... highly irregular.'

Leo turned to Luigi: 'You just stood there. I am meant to be the rookie here.'

Luigi's response to this observation was to turn a shade of indignant red that competed with the hydraulic fluid coating the tunnel walls, push himself upright from behind the cables, and deliver approximately ninety seconds of wounded professional explanation: critical tactical observation, structural integrity monitoring, analysis of patrol patterns, the electromagnetic pulse grenade that was being prepared and would have worked in three more seconds, the recklessness of bypassing secondary containment protocols. Waluigi must interrupt Luigi's defense to note that E. Gadd's assessment immediately corroborated it: the execution was statistically improbable for a novice, undeniably efficient, and completely unscientific. If the hydraulic fluid had been pressurized with volatile mana-ether rather than standard lubricant, Leo's suction burst would have vaporized the entire tunnel. E. Gadd stated this factually. He was disappointed by the lack of scientific rigor, but his hands trembled with relief. Then, in a moment that perfectly encapsulates survival in the Long Dark, E. Gadd reached down into the leaking wreckage of a Guild security construct that they had just illegally destroyed and scavenged a glowing copper coil, stuffing it into a specimen jar.Waluigi must clarify why this specific action matters, and correct a previous lapse in his own analytical framing. Waluigi is reading this from a desk decades later, but to understand E. Gadd in that moment, one must understand the economics of the infrastructure collapse. In 963 BF, a functional copper mana-coil from a Guild golem was not just a scientific curiosity. It was a high-capacity power conduit. In a city operating on thirty percent emergency power, where heating crystals were dead and standard batteries had long since drained, that coil was a priceless asset. Waluigi notes this as an act of calculated survival. E. Gadd was not merely a distracted academic; he was a man who understood that in the Long Dark, when you found a functional energy source, you extracted it immediately, regardless of the imminent danger. The alarms were likely seconds away from triggering. The golem's patrol cycle failure would be detected by the central hub. But E. Gadd took the time to pry the component loose, because the component meant power, and power meant life. Once the coil was secured in his satchel, E. Gadd ordered the retreat. The sprint through the remainder of the maintenance tunnel was not a clean escape. Waluigi’s reconstruction of the field notes reveals a frantic, physically punishing ordeal. The floor was coated in slick, glowing blue hydraulic fluid. The air was heavy with the metallic scent of the ruined golem. Leo had to navigate this uneven, treacherous surface while bearing the shifting, massive weight of the Prototype-X on his back. Every step threatened to send him slipping into the rusted pipework. Luigi ran with one hand gripping his own standard-issue Poltergust and the other pressing against the wall, constantly checking over his shoulder for the red glow of a backup security unit. E. Gadd led the way, his heavy boots splashing through the oil, his lantern casting erratic, terrifying shadows against the copper wiring. They were racing against the station's internal logic systems. It was only a matter of minutesperhaps secondsbefore the central terminal registered the golem's catastrophic pressure loss. ## Part Seven: The Main Terminal and the Departure  Approximately the Fourteenth Hour and Thirty MinutesThey burst from the service corridor into the Legion Line's main transit hub. The transition was violent. They moved from dark, cramped, oil-slicked silence into a sprawling, cavernous expanse of polished steel, flickering overhead lights, and the heavy, bone-rattling low-frequency pulse of the Maglev tracks. Luigi's reaction to this space was immediate, paralyzing terror. He stumbled into the light, leaning heavily against a cold metal bench, gasping for air. He explicitly stated that the bright lights and open space were worse than the tunnel because there was 'nowhere to hide.' Waluigi understands this completely, and it is crucial to document why Luigi was correct. Before 962 BF, bright light in a public transit hub meant safety. It meant civilization, order, and security. In the Long Dark, bright light in a Guild-controlled sector meant exposure. It meant you were visible. Across the vast platform, armored security droids paced the elevated walkways, their red sensor beams sweeping the crowds like lighthouse beams over a stormy sea. To be in the light in 963 BF was to invite the attention of authorities who were authorized to use lethal force to maintain the rationing systems. Luigi's fear was perfectly calibrated to the new reality: darkness was where things with teeth lived, but the light was where the Guild's executioners lived. In this era, both were equally lethal.E. Gadd, momentarily forgetting his own credentials in the rush of adrenaline, panicked when Leo asked how they were boarding. He frantically patted down his pockets, a flurry of clinking vials and discarded half-eaten biscuits, before finally producing the Guild Clearance Token. He held the burnished gold medallion up like a shield against the sweeping droid sensors. He commanded Leo to wipe the existential dread off his face, declaring they would board the train under the guise of a geological survey team. As they moved toward the boarding ramp of the armored Maglev Expressa massive, hissing behemoth of brass and dark iron venting thick plumes of white steamLeo experienced an internal thought that Waluigi has extracted from the psychological overlay of the field notes. It is a brief thought, but Waluigi must freeze the narrative to examine it, because it is the most revealing piece of data in the entire file regarding Leo's worldview and the generational trauma of the Long Dark.Leo thought: *Mario could've stopped this. If only he didn't run away.*Waluigi has analyzed this sentence extensively. It is staggering in its historical implications.Consider the context. Mario is the Kingdom's defining legend. For decades, he was the fixed point around which all crisis resolution revolved. Then came the assassination of Princess Peach in 955 BF. The Toadsmith Incident. The descent into a grinding, brutal civil war. And finally, the catastrophic failure of the Star Road in 962 BF, plunging the world into the freezing misery of the Long Dark. Throughout the worst fourteen months in the history of the Mushroom Kingdom, Mario has been absent. Unseen. Unheard from.But Leo did not think Mario was dead. He did not think Mario was captured by the Iron Legion, or fighting a shadow war behind enemy lines. Leo thought Mario *ran away*. To the Long Dark generationthe youth coming of age in the freezing, rationing, dying world of 963 BFthe absence of the great hero was not perceived as a tactical reality. It was perceived as abandonment. Mario, the man who had saved them from everything else, had looked at the infrastructure collapse, realized it could not be solved by jumping on a turtle, and chosen to flee. This resentment, this profound ideological wound, was the armor Leo wore. It explains his coldness. It explains his fast processing speed and lack of panic. He was not waiting for a hero to save him, because he believed the hero had deserted them. He believed they were entirely on their own.They boarded the train.E. Gadd ushered them past the mechanical conductor droid, using the Clearance Token to secure access to what he called a 'strategically advantageous position.' This turned out to be a cramped, dirty, private observation nook tucked against a ventilation shaft in the very last car, partially obscured by a heavy velvet curtain. The heavy pneumatic doors hissed shut, sealing them inside a vibrating, ozone-scented iron box. The train lurched forward, plunging into the dark tunnels of the mountain pass.Luigi collapsed onto the stiff wooden bench. He told Leo to focus on his breathing. And then, Luigi did something that requires specific economic and psychological documentation: he reached into his pocket, pulled out a small, crumpled piece of hard candy with trembling fingers, and offered it to Leo.Sugar helps with the shock, Luigi said softly. It helped Mario once.Waluigi wants to be extremely clear about what this gesture meant in 963 BF. Sugar was not a casual commodity. The agricultural supply chains that brought sugar cane to Toad Town had been severed for eight years by the civil war, and whatever reserves existed had been frozen or hoarded by the Mages Guild when the Star Road failed. Sugar was pure, fast-burning calories. In the Hoarfrost Winter of the Long Dark, calories were body heat. Calories were literal survival. For Luigi to give away a piece of sugar to a trainee he had met an hour ago was an act of profound, self-sacrificing generosity. And he referenced Mario. While Leo was silently despising Mario for running away, Luigi was invoking his brother's name as a comfort mechanism, passing on a lesson Mario had taught him. The contrast between Leo's bitter resentment and Luigi's enduring, tragic devotion, occupying the exact same physical space on that train compartment, is the emotional core of this expedition. Luigi still believed in the brother who had left him alone in a dying world. Leo chewed the sugar. As a reflex of a pre-collapse mindset, he began looking around the seat for a dinner menu.He did not find a menu. He found a stiff piece of parchmenta topographical transit map of the rail line. E. Gadd snatched the map immediately, his magnifying glass hovering over the parchment. He instantly identified operational hazards: Blackwood Pass, a deep subterranean trench marked with a skull-and-crossbones, notorious for signal interference. If they lost contact with station HQ there, they would be flying blind through contested territory. When Leo asked about the train's amenities, E. Gadd laughed a harsh, wheezing laugh. He pointed to the fine print on the map. The Maglev Express did not serve dinner. It featured an automated vending unit in the dining car that dispensed 'Nutrient Slurry' and dehydrated crackers. Waluigi pauses on this detail. The Mushroom Kingdom was once a civilization defined by its abundancefeasts, banquets, endless supplies of fresh food. Now, its elite Mages Guild operatives, traveling on a high-security armored train to save a village from spectral annihilation, were expected to sustain themselves on heavily rationed, machine-dispensed sludge. This was the texture of life in the second year of the Long Dark.Before the grim reality of the nutrient slurry could fully settle upon the group, the operational environment changed again, instantly and violently.A heavy, rhythmic *thud-thud-thud* sounded from the ceiling of the compartment.E. Gadd froze. The train was moving at tremendous speed through a subterranean mountain pass. The sound was not the wind. It was not a loose bolt. It was the distinct, heavy sound of sharp, multi-jointed limbs scraping against the metal exterior of the train's roof. E. Gadd reached into his lab coat and retrieved a brass-encased ecto-meter. He flicked it on. The needle on the gauge violently slammed all the way to the right, pinning itself deep into the red zone. A massive spectral density spike. Directly above their heads.Stay low, E. Gadd whispered, his face pale under the flickering compartment lamp, gripping Leo's sleeve. If that pressure seal on the ceiling fails, we won't be worrying about dinner; we'll be worrying about whether our souls are still attached to our bodies!Waluigi's analysis of the departure phase concludes here. The transit phase had officially begun. They had successfully navigated the human threatsthe Guild checkpoints, the failing infrastructure, the security golems, and the crowded terminal. But they were now moving through the Long Dark, trapped in a sealed iron box traveling at high speed, and the Long Dark had finally found them. What follows on the roof of the Maglev Express is an entirely different operational paradigm.
